passages.title: The Book is truth; signs across creation
passages.tafsir:
Sūrah ar-Raʿd opens by setting two claims side by side: what has been sent down to Muhammad ﷺ is the truth, and the visible world is evidence that the One who sent it is One. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that this sūrah is Makkan with forty-three verses, and that its running subjects are the truth of the Holy Qurʼān, *tawḥīd* (Allah's oneness), *risālah* (prophethood), and answers to the doubts raised against them. Ayah 1 makes the claim. Ayat 2–4 then take the reader outdoors — the sky overhead, the sun and moon that have never once broken step, the ground underfoot, neighbouring plots watered with one water whose fruit still differs in taste — and let creation argue the case: *the Book is true* → *look at what your eyes already accept* → *so be certain you will meet your Lord*.

## Alif Lām Mīm Rā

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is direct about the opening letters: they are *al-ḥurūf al-muqaṭṭaʿāt*, "the isolated letters," whose meaning is known to Allah alone. The Ummah has not been informed of it, and it is not appropriate for Muslims at large to indulge in investigations about them.

Ibn Kathīr, pointing back to his discussion at the start of Sūrat al-Baqarah, draws out what they nevertheless *establish*: every sūrah that begins with these separate letters goes on to affirm that the Qurʼān is miraculous and is evidence that it is a revelation from Allah, about which there is no doubt or denying.

## "And what has been sent down to you from your Lord"

Ayah 1 names two things joined by "and": **"These are the verses of the Book"** *and* **"what has been sent down to you from your Lord."** It is possible that both phrases mean the Qurʼān itself. But the connective *wāw of ʿaṭf* obviously requires that the two be *distinct* things. On that reading, "the Book" is the Qurʼān, and "what has been sent down to you" is the revelation (*waḥy*) given to the Prophet ﷺ **other than** the Qurʼān — because, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, it goes without saying that the revelation sent to him was not restricted to the Qurʼān alone. The Qurʼān says of him, **"Nor does he speak out of desire"** (53:3): it is a message revealed to him from Allah. So the orders he gave beyond what appears in the Qurʼān are likewise from Allah.

What is the difference? Maʿārif answers with two precise terms: the Qurʼān is *matluww* — "recited" — and the other revelation is *ghayr matluww*, "not recited." In the Qurʼān both the meanings **and the words** are from Allah, whereas in the rules of conduct (*aḥkām*) the Prophet ﷺ gave in ḥadīth, the meanings are without doubt revealed from Allah but the words are not. Therefore they cannot be recited in ṣalāh.

So in one clause the ayah places both the Book and the injunctions given to the Prophet ﷺ under the same word: *al-ḥaqq*, the truth. The verse means, in Maʿārif's summary, that the Qurʼān and the injunctions sent down to the Prophet ﷺ are all true, and in them there is no room for doubt.

## "But most people do not believe"

Ibn Kathīr sets this beside **"And most of mankind will not believe, even if you desire it eagerly"** (12:103), and comments that even after this clear, plain and unequivocal explanation most men will still not believe — due to their rebellion, stubbornness and hypocrisy. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names the quieter cause: most people, *due to their lack of concern and deliberation*, do not come around to believing.

That diagnosis makes ayat 2–4 necessary, and Maʿārif says so at the second verse: that Allah exists and that He is One is emphasised there, and *the proof stands obvious* — look at what has been created and ponder over the matchless mastery with which everything was created, and one can come to only one conclusion, that their Maker has absolute power over everything and controls all creations and universes as the master. If the illness is inattention rather than thin evidence, the treatment is not a new argument but a compelled look.

## The argument overhead

**"Allah is the One who raised the heavens without pillars that you can see."** Ibn Kathīr reads this as a declaration of Allah's perfect ability and infinite authority: by His leave, order and power He has elevated the heavens high above the earth, far out of reach. He describes them as nested, each surrounding the one beneath it through to the seventh — citing **"It is Allah who has created seven heavens and of the earth the like thereof"** (65:12) — with five hundred years between each and five hundred years of thickness for each.

**A genuine difference among the scholars.** The phrase *bi-ghayri ʿamadin tarawnahā* can be read two ways, and Ibn Kathīr reports both:

- **"There are pillars, but you cannot see them"** — the view he attributes to Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah and several other scholars.
- **"There are no pillars at all — as you can see."** Iyās bin Muʿāwiyah said, "The heaven is like a dome over the earth," meaning without pillars; something similar was reported from Qatādah.

Ibn Kathīr judges the second meaning better for this part of the ayah, especially in light of **"He withholds the heaven from falling on the earth except by His permission"** (22:65). On that reading the word *tarawnahā*, "that you can see," is itself the proof: look up, there is nothing there. And that meaning, he says, best affirms Allah's ability and power.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses on that same "you see them," alongside **"and at the sky, how it has been raised"** (88:18), and observes that the physicists' account of the blue overhead — an effect of light and dark intermingling — does not stand counter to it; it also allows, citing *Rūḥ al-Maʿānī*, that where the Qurʼān speaks of "seeing the sky" the expression may be figurative, the sky's existence standing proved under decisive arguments and so as good as seen.

## "Then He rose above the Throne"

On **thumma istawā ʿalā al-ʿarsh**, Ibn Kathīr refers back to his treatment at 7:54 and states the rule plainly: it is to be accepted as it is, *without altering it, without equating it with creation, without annulling its meaning, and without attempts to explain its true nature* — "Allah is glorified and praised from all that they attribute to Him." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same in its own words: this mode of taking over the Seat of Power is beyond human comprehension and understanding it is impossible; here it is sufficient to believe that this *istiwāʼ* is something matching with the Divine Status as due.

## The sun and the moon: obedience you can set a clock by

**"He has subjected the sun and the moon, each running for an appointed term."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān unpacks *sakhkhara*, "subjugated": both are constantly doing exactly what they have been assigned to do. Thousands of years have gone by with never the least increase or decrease in their movement; they do not get tired.

"To an appointed term" carries two possible meanings, and both commentaries give them:

- **Until the Hour.** They continue their course until they cease upon the commencement of the Final Hour — Ibn Kathīr cites **"And the sun runs on its fixed course for a term appointed"** (36:38); Maʿārif adds that both move on to that same determined final term, when this whole system of theirs will reach its end. (Ibn Kathīr also reports a second opinion tied to their settling under the Throne after passing the other side of the earth.)
- **Each to its own fixed measure.** Allah has determined a particular speed and orbit for every planet; the moon completes its orbit in one month, the sun in a year.

Ibn Kathīr notes why *these two* are named: they are among the brightest seven heavenly objects, so if Allah subjected these to His power, it is clear that He has also subjected all other heavenly objects. And subjected things are not to be worshipped — **"Prostrate yourselves not to the sun nor to the moon, but prostrate yourselves to Allah who created them"** (41:37); **"His is the creation and the commandment"** (7:54).

Maʿārif presses the point: a machinery moving on a particular orbit at a particular speed for thousands of years with no wear and tear, no breakage, no greasing, no servicing — set beside the revolutionary advancements of science in our day, it is impossible to locate even a thousandth part of it anywhere in the world. This great system of nature is delivering a message, loud and clear: there certainly is some Being who has made, moved and maintained it, far beyond the reach of human perception and intelligence.

## "He manages all affairs" — and we mostly rearrange

*Yudabbir al-amr.* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: if a man so pleased with the ways and means that make things work for him would open his eyes, he would realise that his plans and measures could neither create nor make things in the real sense; the whole outcome of his efforts is no more than learning how to make the best use of what Allah has already created.

Its illustration: you need to build a house. From architect to builder to finisher, hundreds of human beings offer their career and craft, all set to answer your call; the materials lie stacked in stores and shops, ready to be delivered where you want them. Was it within your power to assemble all this on your own by the brute force of your money or measures, and on top of it commission all those human beings into your service? Not even the mightiest government could establish such a system through the force of law. It is Allah alone — *al-Ḥayy, al-Qayyūm*, the Ever-Living, the Self-Sustaining Sustainer of all — who has linked up everything as if in a chain, in a way that everything gets drawn into the desired action.

**"He explains the signs in detail."** Maʿārif offers two senses of *al-āyāt*: the verses of the Qurʼān, revealed in detail and then elaborated and explained through the Prophet ﷺ; or the signs of Allah's most perfect power spread out in the heavens and the earth, even in the very existence of human beings — before our sight all the time and everywhere, so many and so plain. Ibn Kathīr reads it as the signs and clear evidences that testify there is no deity worthy of worship except Him, evidences which prove that He will resurrect creation if He wills, just as He started it.

**"…so that you may be certain of the meeting with your Lord."** Maʿārif spells out the logic: once you have pondered over this universe and its wondrous system, any likelihood of doubting that raising human beings again is beyond Allah's power simply cannot be entertained. And once we realise it is within His power and possible, and that it has been reported by no less a person than the one about whom it is universally settled that he never said anything in his whole life which was not the truth — then no room for doubt remains.

## The argument underfoot

Ibn Kathīr marks the turn: after mentioning the higher worlds, Allah started asserting His power, wisdom and control over the lower parts of the world.

**"He spread out the earth"** — made it spacious in length and width — **"and placed in it firm mountains and rivers."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān addresses the obvious question: "spread out" is not contradictory of the earth being round, because each part of something very big and round appears, when looked at separately, to be nothing but a surface spread out, and the Qurʼān addresses common people in terms of their view of things. As for the mountains, besides providing weight and balance they store and supply water for the whole creation: an unimaginably big storage of water placed on their peaks as a frozen sea, needing no reservoir and no monolithic structures overhead or underground, and unable to go bad. Nature's own underground pipelines then distribute it all over the world — showing up as rivers flowing with their tributaries, or tapped by wells.

**"And of all the fruits He created in it two of a pair."** Ibn Kathīr takes it as two types from every kind of fruit. Maʿārif allows more: fruits of many kinds, each made of two — small and big, red, white, sweet and sour; or "two" as the least number implied where several kinds exist; or male and female, as we know of the date-palm and the papaya, with the possibility open for other trees though not yet proved by relevant research about all of them.

**"He makes the night cover the day."** Maʿārif: He brings the night after the light of the day, as if something bright has been totally screened off from sight. Ibn Kathīr: Allah made the day and night pursue each other — when one is about to depart the other overcomes it, and vice versa — and Allah controls time just as He controls space and matter.

## One water, different fruit

**"In the earth are neighbouring tracts."** Ibn Kathīr reports from Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Saʿīd bin Jubayr, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk and several others that these are plots next to each other, some fertile and producing what benefits people, others dead and salty and producing nothing. It also covers the various colours and types of diverse areas of the earth — red, white, yellow, black; stony, flat, sandy, thick, thin — all made to neighbour each other while preserving their own qualities. All this, he says, indicates the existence of the Creator who does what He wills; there is no deity or lord except Him.

**"…and gardens of vines, and crops, and date-palms, *ṣinwān* and not *ṣinwān*."** *Ṣinwān* means growing into two or three from a single stem, such as figs, pomegranate and dates; *ghayru ṣinwān* means having one stem for every tree, as is the case with most plants. Ibn Kathīr notes the beautiful extension of the word in Arabic: a man's paternal uncle is called the *ṣinw* of his father — two trunks from one root. He cites an authentic ḥadīth in which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to ʿUmar bin al-Khaṭṭāb, "Do you not know that a man's paternal uncle is the *ṣinw* of his father?" (Ibn Kathīr does not name the collection at this point.)

**"…watered with one water, yet We make some of them better than others to eat."** Maʿārif lists what these plants hold in common: they come out of the same land, are watered by the same water, and are touched by the rays of the sun, the glow of the moon and the draft of different winds in a uniform manner — and yet among them there remains the difference of colour and taste and size. Ibn Kathīr piles up that variety: differences of shape, colour, taste, scent, blossoms and even the shape of their leaves; plants very sweet or sour, bitter or mild; some combining several of these attributes so that the taste changes and becomes another taste, by Allah's will; some yellow, red, white, black or blue, and the same may be said of their flowers.

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathīr records that Abū Hurayrah narrated that the Prophet ﷺ commented on **"yet We make some of them better than others to eat"** with the words: *"The Daqal, the Persian, the sweet, the bitter…"* — naming varieties of date and of taste. At-Tirmidhī collected this ḥadīth and said, "Ḥasan Gharīb."

Maʿārif draws the conclusion: despite their being in such proximity to each other, the varied difference among them is a strong and clear proof that this whole system of creation is operating under the command of someone who is wise and knows how to plan, manage and run His creation. It adds its own objection to those who would explain it as nothing but the stages of material development: if all matter is common, how could we explain the element of difference among them? One fruit grows on a tract of land in one season while another grows in the other; on one single branch of one tree the fruits could differ in kind, size and taste.

## Two audiences, two verbs

Ayah 3 closes with **"signs for a people who *reflect*"** (*yatafakkarūn*) — Ibn Kathīr: those who reflect on Allah's signs and the evidences of His wisdom; Maʿārif: many signs of Allah's most perfect power are present all over for those who care to think about and deliberate in the arrangement and system of this whole universe. Ayah 4 closes with **"signs for a people who *understand*"** (*yaʿqilūn*) — those, in Ibn Kathīr's phrase, who have sound reasoning. Maʿārif catches the sting: by saying the signs are "for a people who understand," the hint released is that those who do not think about these things are not the people of understanding at all — no matter how highly they are rated and advertised for their intellect and intelligence.

## Living it

- **Take the Sunnah as seriously as the Book.** On Maʿārif's reading, ayah 1 calls both *al-ḥaqq*. The difference is that one is recited and the other is not — not that one binds and the other does not.
- **Do not let rejection unsettle you.** "Most people do not believe" is stated by Allah as a fact, alongside 12:103. Truth is not measured by headcount.
- **Look, deliberately.** The failure ayah 1 diagnoses is lack of concern and deliberation. The remedy of ayat 2–4 is to stop and actually consider the sky, the sun's punctuality, the ground, the neighbouring plots watered with one water — until reflection hardens into certainty about meeting Allah.
- **Hold your own competence loosely.** *He manages all affairs.* Your best planning only arranges what He created.
- **Let the differences preach to you.** Same water, different fruit: the variety in the world is not noise. It is deliberate, and it is signed.

passages.title: The deniers' objections: resurrection, punishment, signs
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads ayat 5–7 as a single block: a refutation of the doubts the disbelievers raised about prophethood, with a warning of punishment for the deniers added alongside. Three doubts are answered in turn — *resurrection is absurd*, *then bring on the punishment you threaten*, *then show us the miracle we demand*. After ayah 7, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, the surah returns in ayah 8 to its principal theme of tawhid — the Oneness of Allah — which had been running from the beginning of the surah.

## Ayah 5: the objection that is stranger than any wonder

The ayah opens by turning a mirror on the Prophet's ﷺ own astonishment: *if anything should amaze you, then amazing is their saying, "When we are dust, shall we indeed be in a new creation?"*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān unpacks what the Prophet ﷺ might reasonably have found astonishing. Here were people who had seen clear signs that he was a prophet of Allah and still refused him — while at the same time they went on believing in lifeless rocks that have neither sense nor consciousness, that cannot bring benefit or harm to their own selves, and so could hardly be expected to grant anything to anyone else. That is astonishing enough. But the ayah says: if that amazes you, here is something more amazing still — their denial of being raised again.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān identifies this as the first of their three doubts: they held that returning to life after death, and the whole idea of accounting and retribution on the Day of Resurrection, was improbable and irrational — and on that basis they used to belie the prophets and reject their claim to prophethood. The Qur'an records the doubt in their own mocking words elsewhere: *"Come, we shall introduce you to a man who tells you that you, once dead, shall be shredded into pieces and the molecules of the earth you are made of shall also spread out all over the earth, then, at that time, you shall be created anew"* (34:7).

**Why the denial is the stranger of the two.** Ibn Kathir sets out the argument. These people admit that Allah originated the creation of all things and brought them into existence after they were nothing. They witness the signs and evidences He has placed in His creation, all of them testifying that He is able to do everything. And then they deny that He will resurrect the world anew — even though they already admit to what is more amazing than the thing they reject. It is an obvious fact to every sane and knowledgeable person, Ibn Kathir says, that creating the heavens and the earth is a greater feat than creating human beings, and that the One who has originated creation is more able to resurrect it anew. He brings the Qur'an's own statement of it: "Do they not see that Allah, Who created the heavens and the earth, and was not wearied by their creation, is able to give life to the dead? Yes, He surely is able to do all things" (46:33).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that our ayah does not spell out the reasoning explicitly — because the preceding ayat of this surah have already done it, describing the wondrous manifestations of Allah's most perfect power and proving that He is the master of absolute power. He brought the entire creation from the state of non-being into the state of being, and then endowed into the being of everything so many varied elements of wisdom that human beings cannot even comprehend them fully. Once that is granted, the conclusion follows on its own: a Being who can make something come into existence for the first time out of total nothingness will hardly have difficulty in making it come into existence once again. Even in our own small experience, making a thing the first time means removing difficulties; making the same thing again is easier. What is really surprising, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, is that these disbelievers do seem to believe that the Creator created the whole universe with limitless wisdom — how then can they consider its re-creation improbable and irrational?

**The real sticking point — scattered dust.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is honest about where the deniers' imagination actually jams. Perhaps the big problem before them is what happens *after* death. Dust returns to dust; whatever human beings are composed of gets spread out all over the earth; winds carry the particles far and wide, and other causes, agents and means help human remains get dispersed universally. Then comes the promised Day, the Qiyamah. How, they wonder, could all that scattered dust be put together — and even if gathered, how could they be made to rise again as they were?

What they fail to see, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers, is that the form in which they exist right now holds the key to their difficulty. Is it not that particles from all over the world lie gathered together in them while they exist? Particles brought by water and wind from the far and near corners of the world get mingled with human intake and become part of a person's body. Most of the time the poor soul is not even aware that the morsel of food going down his throat comes from who knows how many areas of the world — Africa, America, the countries of the Asian continent. There is only One Being who, through His wondrous wisdom and mastery of management, has made every single human being and every animal stand in existence by assembling together scattered particles from all over the world. Now if He can do that today, how can it become difficult for Him tomorrow? Why would He not be capable of reassembling all those scattered particles back into the form they were? And especially so when all the powers of the world — the wind, the water and the rest — are subservient to Him and obey His command. If He elects to beckon the wind, the water and the atmosphere to come forth and deposit all the particles they contain, would they not obey?

**The root error.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names the disease behind the symptom: the disbelievers have simply failed to recognise the power of Allah. They think of His power on the analogy of their own power — measuring what the Creator can do by what a creature can do. Yet everything in the heavens and the earth and in what lies between them possesses a comprehension and consciousness of its relative status in the scheme of the Divine arrangement of things, and moves pointedly under Divine command.

So, in short: what is a matter of surprise is their refusal to believe in the truth of prophethood. And what is still more surprising is their refusal to believe in rising again on the Day of Judgment and having to stand and account for their deeds.

**"They are those who disbelieved in their Lord."** The second half of ayah 5 does not treat this as an intellectual slip. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that these people are not simply refusing to accept a prophet of Allah as such; what they do in reality is deny their very Lord. Ibn Kathir marks the same turn in the passage: having shown how strange the denial is, Allah then describes those who deny Resurrection in the ayah's own words — *they are those who disbelieved in their Lord.*

Their end is described in three strokes. Iron chains (*al-aghlāl*) linking their hands to their necks — Ibn Kathir explains that they will be dragged into the Fire by these chains. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders the same image as shackles placed round their necks. And then: dwellers of the Fire, abiding therein — Ibn Kathir is explicit that they will remain in Hell forever and will never escape it or be removed from it.

## Ayah 6: "hasten the torment rather than grace"

The second doubt was not philosophical but taunting. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states it plainly: *if you are, in reality, the prophet and messenger of Allah, then the warnings of punishment you announce against the opponents of prophets should materialise — why is it that this punishment would not come?* Ayah 6 reports them asking to hasten "the evil before the good"; Ibn Kathir explains that "the evil" here means the punishment. The very demand, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out, shows that they took the coming of Divine punishment as something very far-removed, or virtually impossible.

Ibn Kathir gathers other ayat where the Qur'an records the same demand — "Why do you not bring angels to us if you are of the truthful?" (15:6–8), "And they ask you to hasten on the torment" (29:53–54), "A questioner asked concerning a torment about to befall" (70:1), and "Our Lord! Hasten to us *Qittana*" (38:16), which Ibn Kathir glosses as *our due torment and reckoning*. He adds that they even made it a supplication: "O Allah! If this is indeed the truth from You…" (8:32). They were such rebellious, stubborn disbelievers, Ibn Kathir says, that they asked the Messenger ﷺ to bring them Allah's torment. Set against them, the Qur'an notes the opposite reflex in the believer: "Those who believe not therein seek to hasten it, while those who believe are fearful of it, and know that it is the very truth" (42:18).

**"Exemplary punishments have occurred before them."** The answer comes first as history. The word is *al-mathulāt*; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains it as the plural of *mathula*, meaning a punishment that puts a person in disgrace before everyone and proves to be a lesson for all others. Ibn Kathir reads the ayah as Allah saying: We have already exerted Our punishment on the previous disbelieving nations, and made them a lesson and an example for those who might take heed from their destruction. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presses the point: punishments have really come to pass against people earlier than them, and others witnessed it — so if the punishment is to come to them, why should it be taken as something far out, or impossible?

**Why it has not come yet.** The answer's second half is the weightier one: *your Lord is full of forgiveness for mankind in spite of their wrongdoing.* Were it not for His forbearance and forgiveness, Ibn Kathir says, Allah would indeed have punished them sooner — and he cites, "And if Allah were to punish men for that which they earned, He would not leave a moving creature on the surface of the earth" (35:45). So the non-arrival of punishment, which they treated as an argument against the Prophet ﷺ, is on Ibn Kathir's reading the working of Allah's forbearance: He is full of forgiveness, pardoning and covering the mistakes of people in spite of their wrongdoing and the errors committed night and day.

**And then the balance.** The ayah does not end on forgiveness; it ends with *your Lord is severe in punishment*. Ibn Kathir notes the purpose of this: Allah reminds us that His punishment is severe so that fear and hope are both addressed and mentioned together, as the Qur'an does in many other ayat — "Your Lord is the Owner of vast mercy, and never will His wrath be turned back from the people who are criminals" (6:147); "Verily, your Lord is quick in retribution and certainly He is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful" (7:167); "Declare unto My servants that truly I am the Oft-Forgiving, the Most Merciful. And that My torment is indeed the most painful torment" (15:49–50). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the practical lesson: for people who do not take advantage of that forgiveness and mercy and elect to stick to their disobedience and defiance, He is severe in punishing as well. They should not misunderstand the attributes of Allah's forgiveness and mercy and reach the conclusion that punishment simply cannot come to them.

## Ayah 7: "why is no sign sent down to him?"

The third doubt concerned miracles. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān frames it exactly: as for the miracles of the Prophet ﷺ, they had seen many of them — so the complaint was *why will he not show the specific miracle we demand?* Ibn Kathir describes the same stubbornness: out of their disbelief and stubbornness the idolators asked why a miracle was not sent down to the Messenger ﷺ from his Lord, just like the earlier Messengers; they were being stubborn when they asked him to turn as-Safa into gold, to remove the mountains from around them and replace them with green fields and rivers. Ibn Kathir sets alongside this: "And nothing stops Us from sending the Ayat but that the people of old denied them" (17:59).

**"You are only a warner."** The reply — *innamā anta mundhir* — is short, and it relocates the whole question. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that the showing of a miracle is not within the control of a prophet or messenger; it is directly an act of Allah. It is He who elects to show a miracle, of whatever kind, at any time, and in His wisdom, all as determined by Him alone; He is not restricted by or burdened with anyone's demand or desire. The Prophet ﷺ is there to warn disbelievers against Divine punishment — showing miracles is not his mission. Ibn Kathir puts the same limit on the messenger's responsibility: your duty is only to convey Allah's Message which He has ordered you, and he cites "Not upon you is their guidance, but Allah guides whom He wills" (2:272). *Mundhir* means one who warns: the mission is warning, not miracle-working.

**"And to every people there is a guide."** Ibn Kathir reports that this means for every people there has been a caller — according to Ibn ʿAbbas, as narrated from him by ʿAli bin Abi Talhah — and he supports it with a similar ayah, "And there never was a nation but a warner had passed among them" (35:24); similar has been reported from Qatadah and ʿAbdur-Rahman bin Zayd. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the argument this makes against the objectors: there have been guides for every people among past communities, so the Prophet ﷺ is not the lone prophet. The standard mission of all prophets was to guide their people and warn them of the punishment of Allah — but none of them were given the power and control to show miracles. It is Allah who shows miracles of His choice whenever He chooses to do so.

**A question raised here.** Does "for every people there is a guide" require that a prophet appeared among every people and in every country? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers that the ayah proves no people and no region can remain unvisited by those who call towards Allah and guide people to the straight path — but that guide may be some prophet himself, or someone propagating the call as his deputy. The example given is from Surah Ya-Sin, where two persons were first sent as deputies to the prophet of the time to a certain people (and were prophets in their own right), and then a third was sent to help and support them. So the ayah does not make it necessary to say that a prophet appeared in India; what stands proved is that learned people who carried the call of the Prophet ﷺ and told people about his teachings came to this part of the world as well — and it is already common knowledge that many such guides have appeared here.

## Living it

Three doubts are answered in these ayat. Each one rests on an attitude worth checking in ourselves.

**Measuring Allah by ourselves.** The denial in ayah 5 comes, in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's diagnosis, from thinking of Divine power on the analogy of our own. Whenever something feels impossible for Allah — a heart changing, a body raised from dust — the honest question is whether we are reasoning about Allah's power or about ours.

**Misreading patience as safety.** In ayah 6, they took the non-arrival of punishment as proof it could never come. The correction is to hold two truths together, as the ayah itself does: He is full of forgiveness for people in spite of their wrongdoing, and He is severe in punishment. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān warns explicitly against reading the attributes of forgiveness and mercy as a guarantee that punishment cannot come — hope that does not curdle into presumption, fear that does not collapse into despair.

**Wanting proof on our terms.** In ayah 7 the objectors had already seen many signs; what they wanted was a sign of their own specification. Signs are Allah's to give, at the time and in the manner He chooses, and guidance is Allah's to give. What was placed on the Prophet ﷺ was to convey and to warn — and to leave the outcome where it belongs.

passages.title: Allah's all-encompassing knowledge and guarding angels
passages.tafsir:
**What holds these four ayat together.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān supplies the thread itself, verse by verse: of ayah 8 it says that this matchless knowledge of Allah is an open proof of His Oneness (*tawḥīd*); of ayah 10, that the same perfection in knowledge and power is pointed to "in a particular manner"; of ayah 11, that this is where the point of ayah 10 is elaborated. So the passage moves in a single line: from the most hidden place any of us has ever been — the womb — to the One who knows the unseen and the seen, down to our whispers and our movements after dark, and finally out into the open, where angels are posted around every human being, changing shift, keeping watch.

## Ayah 8 — the womb, where no one else can look

Allah opens with a knowledge no human being has ever shared: **مَا تَحۡمِلُ كُلُّ أُنثَىٰ** — *what every female bears*. Ibn Kathir explains that this is knowledge of the child down to its details: whether male or female, fair or ugly, miserable or happy, whether it will have a long life or a short one. He reads it alongside *And He knows that which is in the wombs* (31:34), *He knows you well when He created you from the earth, and when you were fetuses* (53:32), and *He creates you in the wombs of your mothers: creation after creation in three veils of darkness* (39:6) — meaning, he says, stage after stage.

**The two key words.** The ayah continues: **وَمَا تَغِيضُ ٱلۡأَرۡحَامُ وَمَا تَزۡدَادُ** — *what the wombs decrease and what they increase*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān takes the verb *taghīḍ* in its root sense: to become less, to dry up. Because it is set here against *tazdād* (increase), its meaning at this place is clearly "decrease." But decrease of what? The commentary offers two possibilities and refuses to force a choice:

- **Number** — whether the womb holds only one child or more than one.
- **Term** — in how many months, days and hours the pregnancy will come to birth.

Al-ʿAwfī reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that "what the wombs fall short" refers to **miscarriages**, and "what they increase" refers to carrying the child the full term: some women carry for ten months, others for nine, some terms longer and some shorter — "and all this occurs by His knowledge." Mujāhid explained the decrease differently: the blood a woman loses in pregnancy becomes a cause of decrease in the size and health of the child. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that since the words of the ayah cover decreases *of all kinds*, no contradiction exists between these explanations.

**What the ayah is really claiming.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful here. Whatever opinion a physician gives on this matter, based on clinical indicators and educated guess, "cannot be taken to be any more than strong likelihood or estimate." There are times when things turn out otherwise; even X-rays and more modern imaging techniques fail to unravel the reality of the phenomenon as it is. Real and certain knowledge of that hidden life can be credited to Allah alone. Al-Bukhārī recorded from ʿAbdullāh bin ʿUmar that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: **the Keys of the Ghayb are five, and nobody knows them but Allah** — what will happen tomorrow, what is in the womb, when it will rain, in what land a soul will die, and when the Final Hour will begin. The womb sits in that list of five.

**And yet it is all written.** In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, ʿAbdullāh bin Masʿūd reported that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that the creation of each of us is put together in the mother's womb for forty days, then is a clot of thick blood for a similar period, then a piece of flesh for a similar period; then Allah sends an angel who is ordered to write four things: **his provision, his life span, his deeds, and whether he will be blessed or wretched.** Ibn Kathir cites a further narration in which the angel asks, "O my Lord! Is it a male or a female, miserable or happy, what is its provision and life span?" — and Allah ordains and the angel records it. So the hidden thing is hidden from us, not from Him.

**"Everything with Him is in proportion."** The closing phrase, **وَكُلُّ شَيۡءٍ عِندَهُۥ بِمِقۡدَارٍ**, is the seal on all of it. Qatādah commented: "For a term appointed. Allah has the records of the provisions and terms of His creation and made an appointed term for everything." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it as: there can be no decrease or increase from the norm set with Allah — how many days the child stays in the womb, how long it will then live in the world, and how much sustenance it will receive.

Ibn Kathir reports as an authentic hadith, without naming a collection: one of the daughters of the Prophet ﷺ sent a messenger asking him to come, as her child was dying. He ﷺ sent the messenger back with the words: *whatever Allah takes is for Him and whatever He gives is for Him, and everything with Him has a limited fixed term* — so let her be patient and hope for Allah's reward. The same phrase that proves His knowledge is the phrase you hold on to at a deathbed.

## Ayah 9 — Knower of the unseen and the seen, the Great, the High

Ayah 9 names what ayah 8 demonstrated. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that the theme of the exclusive attributes of the perfection of Allah continues here — a theme that begins earlier than these verses and amounts, in its words, to "an array of proofs concerning the Oneness of Allah."

It then defines the two terms. **Al-ghayb** is that which is absent from the reach of human senses — what cannot be seen with the eyes, heard with the ears, smelled, tasted, or sensed by touch. **Ash-shahādah** stands in contrast to it: what can be found out by those same senses. The exclusive attribute being declared is that Allah knows everything hidden *precisely as* He knows what is manifest, present and existing. Ibn Kathir puts the same point his way: He knows everything the servants see and all that they cannot see, and none of it ever escapes His knowledge — *He surrounds all things in knowledge* (65:12).

**Al-Kabīr and al-Mutaʿāl.** Ibn Kathir glosses them in four words: *al-Kabīr* — greater than everything; *al-Mutaʿāl* — above everything. He adds that Allah has full power over all things, the necks are under His control, and the servants are subservient to Him, willingly or unwillingly.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the lexical sense of each word — *al-kabīr*, the great; *al-mutaʿāl*, the high, the one above — and then the sense conveyed by the two together: that He is great and far above the attributes of what He has created.

The commentary then diagnoses where people went wrong. The disbelievers and polytheists did confess to the great and exalted state of the Being of Allah in a general way, but were misguided by a lack of proper perception when they took Allah **on the analogy of common human beings** and went on to associate with Him attributes far removed from His majesty. It instances the Jews and the Christians attributing a son to Allah; others suggesting for Him a body and its parts just like those of human beings; and still others trying to prove direction and orientation for Him. The fact, it concludes, is that Allah is far above, absolutely pure and free of all such conditions and attributions. Allah has reminded us repeatedly in the Qur'an: **سُبْحَانَ اللَّهِ عَمَّا يَصِفُونَ** — "Allah is pure and free from what these people attribute to Him" (23:91; 37:159).

## Ayah 10 — the whisper and the shout are the same to Him

Now the vast claim of ayah 9 lands on ordinary life. **سَوَآءٞ مِّنكُم مَّنۡ أَسَرَّ ٱلۡقَوۡلَ وَمَن جَهَرَ بِهِۦ** — *alike is the one among you who speaks quietly and the one who speaks aloud*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the line between the two words: *asarra al-qawl* (to speak quietly) derives from *asrār*, meaning secret talk, while *jahr* means open talk. When a person talks so as to be heard by others, that is *jahr*; what he says only for his own hearing is *sirr*. Then the second pair: *mustakhfin*, one who hides, and *sārib*, one who walks his way freely. Night and day, indoors and out, muttered and proclaimed — all four are alike in terms of His knowledge, and, the commentary adds, alike in terms of His power too: no one at all is outside His power and control.

Ibn Kathir supports this with *And if you speak aloud, then verily He knows the secret and that which is yet more hidden* (20:7) and *And Allah knows what you conceal and what you reveal* (27:25). ʿĀʾishah said: "All praise is due to Allah Whose hearing has encompassed all voices! By Allah, she who came to complain about her husband to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was speaking while I was in another part of the room, yet I did not hear some of what she said" — and Allah sent down *Indeed Allah has heard the statement of her that disputes with you concerning her husband and complains to Allah; and Allah hears the argument between you both* (58:1).

Ibn Kathir also brings *Surely, even when they cover themselves with their garments* (11:5) and *Nothing is hidden from your Lord, so much as a speck of dust on the earth or in the heaven, not what is less than that or what is greater, but it is in a Clear Record* (10:61). Concealment, then, is never a state that holds in relation to Allah; it only ever holds between us and each other.

## Ayah 11 — the angels who change shift

**The word.** **مُعَقِّبَٰتٞ** (*muʿaqqibāt*) is the plural of *muʿaqqibah*, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the root sense: a group which comes concurrently behind another group — hence the rendering "replacing each other." **مِّنۢ بَيۡنِ يَدَيۡهِ** literally means "between his two hands," which denotes the direction in front of a person, and **وَمِنۡ خَلۡفِهِۦ** means "behind him" — a security cordon closed at the front and at the back.

**A grammatical detail with meaning.** The phrase **مِنۡ أَمۡرِ ٱللَّهِ** would ordinarily read "from the command of Allah." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, citing Rūḥ al-Maʿānī, that the particle *min* stands here in place of the *bāʾ* of causation, so the sense is *bi-amri-llāh*: **under the command of Allah** — and that in some readings (*qirāʾāt*) of the Qur'an the word is in fact reported as *bi-amri-llāh*. The assignment given to them, in the commentary's words, is that they should protect human beings.

**How the watch is arranged.** Ibn Kathir sets out the picture. There are angels who take turns guarding each servant, some by night and some by day, protecting each person from harm and accidents. There are also angels who take turns recording deeds — the angel to the right records the good deeds, the angel to the left the evil. And there are two who guard, one from in front and one from behind. So: **four angels surround each person by day, replaced by four others at night — two scribes and two guards.**

Ibn Kathir cites as an authentic hadith the description of the handover: angels take turns around you, some at night and some by day, and they all assemble at the Fajr and ʿAṣr prayers; then those who have stayed with you through the night ascend to Allah, who asks them — though He knows the answer better than they do — "How have you left My servants?" and they reply, "As we have found them praying, we have left them praying." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān traces this arrangement of two shifts meeting at Fajr and ʿAṣr to a hadith in the Ṣaḥīḥ of al-Bukhārī: the night guards depart after the Fajr prayer and the daytime guards take over; the day guards leave after ʿAṣr and the night guards resume.

**What exactly are they protecting us from?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gathers several strands:

- From **physical harm**: as reported from Sayyidunā al-Murtaḍā in a hadith of Abū Dāwūd, guardian angels are appointed for every human being, and it is their duty to guard lest a wall or something else fall over them, or they stumble into a ditch or cave, or some animal or man cause them hurt or harm. However, when the will of Allah itself stands enforced against a person condemned to suffer some hardship or calamity, the guarding angels move away from the site (cited from Rūḥ al-Maʿānī).
- From **sin**: from a narration of Sayyidunā ʿUthmān al-Ghanī in a hadith of Ibn Jarīr, we learn that their duty is not limited to worldly protection — they also try to dissuade people from sins, infusing in their hearts the urge to do good and to fear Allah. If a person becomes neglectful of that inspiration and falls into sin anyway, they nevertheless pray for him and try that he should hasten to repent and be cleansed. Only if he takes no warning and refuses to correct himself do they write the sin down in his Book of Deeds.
- From **the jinn**: the well-known Kaʿb al-Aḥbār — described by the commentary as a *Tābiʿī*, that is, one of the generation who came after the Companions — said that should this protective Divine cordon be removed from around human beings, the jinn would make their lives difficult.

Ibn Kathir places alongside this the hadith recorded by Imām Aḥmad from ʿAbdullāh — and collected by Muslim — that every one among you has his companion from the jinn and his companion from the angels. They said, "And you too, O Allah's Messenger?" He ﷺ said: "And I too, except that Allah has helped me against him, so he only orders me to do good."

**Why this follows ayah 10.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says explicitly that ayah 11 elaborates the point of ayah 10: whether a person conceals what he says or discloses it, whether he hides his movement under cover of night or walks openly in broad daylight, there are groups of angels appointed from Allah providing a cordon in front of him and behind him.

## The turning point: change

The rest of ayah 11 states the law that governs when that protection stays and when it lifts: **إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ لَا يُغَيِّرُ مَا بِقَوۡمٍ حَتَّىٰ يُغَيِّرُواْ مَا بِأَنفُسِهِمۡ** — *Allah does not change what is in a people until they change what is in themselves.*

Ibn Kathir narrates from Ibn Abī Ḥātim, from Ibrāhīm, that Allah revealed to a Prophet from among the Children of Israel: "Say to your nation: every people of a village or a house who used to obey Allah but changed their behaviour to disobeying Him — then He will take away from them what they like and exchange it for what they dislike." Ibrāhīm said that this statement has its proof in Allah's Book, and quoted this very ayah.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads it in exactly that direction: Allah does not change the state of peace and security enjoyed by a people into a state of distress and instability until those people themselves change their deeds and ways into evil and disorder. And when a whole people commit themselves to rank defiance and disobedience, Allah too changes His way with them — the posse of protection He posted is called off duty, and then, as the ayah says, **وَإِذَا أَرَادَ ٱللَّهُ بِقَوۡمٖ سُوٓءٗا فَلَا مَرَدَّ لَهُۥ** — when Allah intends evil for a people there is no way it can be averted, and there is no patron for them other than Him.

**A note on the popular reading.** The ayah is often quoted in the opposite direction — that no positive revolution appears among a people unless they themselves set about correcting conditions — and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records this as a common explanation, quoting a very popular Urdu couplet built on it. What is said there is, no doubt, correct to a certain extent, but it is not the sense of this ayah. Where it is correct, it is correct as a general principle: for a person with no intention of correcting himself there is no promise of help and support from Allah; the promise holds on the condition that a person himself thinks and does something about it, as in *those who strive in Us, We shall surely guide them to Our paths* (29:69). But, the commentary adds beautifully, Divine **blessings** are not bound by that restriction; at times they come even without it. Take our own existence and its countless blessings — eyes, nose, ears, the rest of this most perfect body — none of it the outcome of our effort, none of it ever prayed for, all of it given. What effort *does* determine is desert: the right to deserve blessings cannot be had without making one's own effort to earn it, and a people who keep waiting for Divine rewards without putting in the due effort and deed are, in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's phrase, engaged in nothing but self-deception.

## Living with these ayat

Three things this passage asks of a believer:

1. **Let the unseen be His.** The five keys named in the hadith recorded by al-Bukhārī mark the boundary of what any expert, scan or forecast can deliver. Take the best knowledge available — and hold it, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, as strong likelihood or estimate, not certainty.
2. **Take *bi-miqdār* to heart when it hurts.** Term, provision, lifespan: measured out and recorded. The Prophet ﷺ sent that very truth to his own grieving daughter, with the instruction to be patient and to hope for Allah's reward.
3. **Live as one who is heard and accompanied.** Nothing said in a locked room is off the record; and the angel who records is joined by an angel working to keep you from needing it recorded — infusing the urge to do good, praying for you when you fall, waiting for your repentance before writing anything down. And what the departing shift reports at Fajr and ʿAṣr is simply how you were found.

passages.title: Storm signs, powerless idols, and universal prostration
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** These four ayat take you outside, under a storm sky, and press one question: who actually runs this world, and who is worth calling on? Ayah 12 shows Allah showing you the lightning and bringing up the water-laden clouds; ayah 13 has thunder itself glorifying Him and the angels glorifying Him out of awe of Him, while He sends down bolts that strike whom He wills — and the deniers stand there disputing about Him. Ayah 14 then draws the contrast: the call that is true is the call to Him; every other call is a thirsty man's hand reaching for water it will never touch. Ayah 15 closes the circle — everything in the heavens and the earth already prostrates to Him, willingly or unwillingly, down to the shadows that lean at the beginning and the end of the day. Power, praise, prayer, prostration: one argument in four moves.

## The sky that frightens and the sky that feeds

Ibn Kathir opens simply: Allah has full power over *al-barq* — lightning — "the bright light that originates from within clouds." He notes that Ibn Jarir recorded that Ibn 'Abbas once wrote to Abu Al-Jald asking about the meaning of *al-barq*, and the answer came back: **it is water.** The flash is not the point; what the flash announces is.

That is exactly why the Arabic gives lightning two effects at once: **خَوْفًا وَطَمَعًا — "as a fear and as a hope."** Qatadah unpacks the pairing beautifully: "Fear for travellers, for they feel afraid of its harm and hardship, and hope for residents, awaiting its blessing and benefit and anticipating Allah's provisions." One sky, two hearts. The man out on the open road sees danger; the man at home over his fields sees mercy on its way. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the same point from the other side — the lightning can become a matter of fear, in case it destroys what it strikes, and it carries a dimension of hope too, raising the expectation that rains may follow, rains which support animal and human life. Fear and hope are not competing readings of the sky. They are two true responses to one sign, and the commentators give both without cancelling either.

**"And it is He Who brings up the clouds, heavy (with water)."** The word for the clouds here is *ath-thiqāl* — the heavy ones. Ibn Kathir explains: He originates the clouds that are heavy and close to the ground because of being laden with rain; and Mujahid said the same — this part of the ayah is about clouds heavy with rain. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in the whole journey: He is the One who lifts heavy, huge clouds up from the surface of the sea as the monsoons, carries these water-laden clouds post-haste through the atmosphere to places near and far off, and has them deliver their rains over the lands He chooses, in accordance with His decree and corresponding to the measure He has determined. Nothing about that chain is idle. Every stage is a choice made by Someone.

## Thunder is not noise, it is praise

**"And Ar-Ra'd (thunder) glorifies and praises Him, and so do the angels because of His awe."**

What does it mean for thunder to glorify Allah? Both commentaries send you to the same verse: *"And there is not a thing but glorifies His praise"* (17:44). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān quotes it in full — "there is nothing in the heavens and the earth which does not glorify Allah, but they do not understand their glorification." So the *tasbīh* that thunder performs — *tasbīh* meaning to proclaim Allah's purity, declaring Him free of every defect, along with His praise — is the same universal *tasbīh* that all created things perform. Creation is not silent; we are simply not the ones who understand it.

On the word itself, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that in Arabic usage *ar-ra'd* refers to the sound of the clouds generated by their collision. It also mentions that it appears in some narrations that *Ar-Ra'd* is the name of the angel appointed to bring the rains — and on that reading, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, the reciting of *tasbīh* is obvious: an angel is doing exactly what angels do. The source offers both senses without forcing a choice.

Ibn Kathir preserves a striking narration here, recorded by **Imam Ahmad**, going back to a man of the tribe of Ghifar who had accompanied the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. The setting is worth picturing. Ibrahim bin Sa'd relates that his father was sitting next to Hamid bin 'Abdur Rahman in the masjid when a man of Ghifar passed by; Hamid sent someone to invite him over, and said to the man beside him, "My nephew! Make space for him between me and you, for he had accompanied Allah's Messenger ﷺ." The man then reported that he heard the Prophet ﷺ say:

> **"Verily, Allah originates the clouds, and they speak in the most beautiful voice and laugh in the most beautiful manner."**

Ibn Kathir comments — "and Allah has the best knowledge" — that the cloud's voice is in reference to thunder and its laughter is the lightning. And Musa bin 'Ubaydah narrated that Sa'd bin Ibrahim said of the rain: none has a better smile than it, nor more comforting voice; its smile is lightning and its voice is thunder. Sit with that image the next time a storm rolls in. What sounds to you like violence is, in the description the Prophet ﷺ gave, something closer to speech and laughter.

**"…and so do the angels because of His awe."** *Min khīfatihi* — out of fear of Him; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders it "out of His awe." The angels glorify Him in awe of Him. Now hold that beside the last clause of the ayah, where human beings are *disputing* about Him. The contrast is the point.

## The bolts that fall: "He strikes whom He wills"

**"He sends the thunderbolts, and therewith He strikes whom He wills."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that *aṣ-ṣawāʿiq* is the plural of *ṣāʿiqah*, the name of the thunderbolt that strikes the earth: it is Allah who sends these down upon the earth, and with them He strikes whom He wills. Ibn Kathir reads this as punishment — He sends thunderbolts as punishment upon whom He wills — and he adds that this is why thunderbolts increase as time comes to an end.

Here the sources give the passage its most vivid backdrop — a real incident from the Prophet's ﷺ life in Madinah, narrated by **Al-Hafiz Abu Al-Qasim At-Tabarani** on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas.

Two men, **Arbad bin Qays** and **'Amir bin At-Tufayl**, came to Madinah, to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and sat where he was sitting. 'Amir asked, "O Muhammad! What will you give me if I embrace Islam?" He ﷺ answered, *"You will have the rights and duties of all Muslims."* Not enough. "Will you make me your successor if I embrace Islam?" He ﷺ replied, *"That is not your right, nor your people's right. However, I could appoint you a commander of the horsemen."* 'Amir pushed further — he was already the commander of the horsemen of Najd; let him have control over the desert and the Prophet ﷺ keep the cities. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ refused. As they left, 'Amir threatened: "By Allah! I will fill it with horses and men." The reply was a single short sentence: *"Rather, Allah will prevent you."*

Then came the plot. 'Amir told Arbad: I will keep Muhammad busy talking, and you strike him with the sword; if he is killed, the Muslims will agree to take blood money rather than wage war over his murder, and we will pay it. Arbad agreed, and they returned. 'Amir called the Prophet ﷺ aside — "O Muhammad! Stand next to me so that I can talk to you" — and the two stood by a wall in conversation. Arbad wanted to grab his sword, and his hand froze the moment it touched the handle; he could not draw the blade from its sheath. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ looked at Arbad, realised what he was doing, and departed.

The two left and stopped at Al-Harrah of Waqim, where Sa'd bin Mu'adh and Usayd bin Hudayr came out calling, "Come, O enemies of Allah! May Allah curse you." They fled until they reached the Riqm area, where **Allah struck Arbad with a bolt of lightning and he met his demise.** 'Amir got further, to the Kharim area, where Allah sent an open ulcer that struck him. He spent that night taking refuge in the house of a woman of Banu Salul, touching the ulcer and saying, "An ulcer as big as a camel's hump, while I am at the house of a woman from Bani Salul, seeking to bring my death in her house!" He rode his horse to head home, and died while riding it.

In this narration, the ayat just before our passage — from *"Allah knows what every female bears"* (13:8) to *"and they will find besides Him no protector"* (13:11) — came down in the case of these two men. Ibn 'Abbas commented that the angels in succession guard Muhammad ﷺ by the command of Allah; then, mentioning the demise of Arbad by Allah's command, he recited: ***"He sends the thunderbolts."***

So the storm imagery in this passage is not abstract. A man plotted the murder of the Prophet ﷺ, his hand was frozen on the hilt, and the sky came down on him.

**"…yet they dispute about Allah."** Ibn Kathir: they doubt Allah's greatness and that there is no deity worthy of worship except Him. That is the astonishing thing this ayah exposes — the thunder is glorifying Him, the angels are in awe of Him, the bolts are falling by His command, and the human being is still standing there arguing.

**"And He is Mighty in strength and Severe in punishment" — *shadīd al-miḥāl*.** This phrase repays attention. Ibn Kathir, following the Tafsir of Ibn Jarir At-Tabari, takes it as the severity of Allah's torment against those who rebel against Him, defy Him and persist in disbelief, and 'Ali bin Abi Talib said plainly that *al-miḥāl* means His punishment is severe. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the word carries a **triple sense**: stratagem and plan; retribution and punishment; and power. All three fit the story just told — men made a plan, and Allah's plan overtook it. Ibn Kathir puts a similar ayah beside it: *"So they plotted a plot, and We planned a plan, while they perceived not. Then see how was the end of their plot! Verily, We destroyed them and their nation all together"* (27:50–51). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's summary is the lesson: these people busy themselves with debates and altercations about the truth of Allah's Oneness, while Allah has the ultimate power, whose plan overtakes all and against which nothing works.

## From the Sunnah: what to do when you hear thunder

The passage turns weather into worship, and the Sunnah shows the reader how.

**Imam Ahmad** recorded that Salim bin 'Abdullah narrated from his father that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to say upon hearing the thunder and thunderbolts:

> **"O Allah! Do not kill us with Your anger, nor destroy us with Your torment, and save us before that."**

Ibn Kathir notes this was also recorded by **At-Tirmidhi**, by **Al-Bukhari in Al-Adab Al-Mufrad**, by **An-Nasa'i in 'Amal Al-Yawm wal-Laylah**, and by **Al-Hakim in Al-Mustadrak**. Learn it. It is short, and it turns a moment of instinctive unease into a moment of turning back to Allah.

And 'Abdullah bin Az-Zubayr, when he used to hear thunder, **would stop talking** and supplicate: "All praise is to He Whom Ar-Ra'd glorifies and praises, and so do the angels because of His awe" — the ayah itself, made into a supplication. Then he would say: **"This is a stern warning to the people of earth."** Ibn Kathir notes that Malik collected this in Al-Muwatta', and Al-Bukhari in Al-Adab Al-Mufrad.

There is one more narration here that cuts deep. **Imam Ahmad** recorded that Abu Hurayrah said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that our Lord, the Exalted and Most High, said:

> **"Had My servants obeyed Me, I would have given them rain by night and the sun by day, and would not have made them hear the sound of the Ra'd (thunder)."**

Rain by night, sun by day, and no sound of thunder at all — that, in this narration, is what obedience would have earned. Worth sitting with the next time the sky is loud.

## The true call, and the hand that never reaches the water

**"For Him is the Word of Truth"** — *lahu daʿwat al-ḥaqq*. 'Ali bin Abi Talib said this is in reference to **Tawhid** — the affirmation of Allah's Oneness — as Ibn Jarir At-Tabari records; and Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, and Malik — narrating it from Muhammad bin Al-Munkadir — said it means **"Lā ilāha illallāh."** The call that has truth in it, the invocation that lands, is the one directed to Allah alone.

Against that, Allah sets one of the most physical images in the Qur'an: those who call on others besides Him are answered no more than **"one who stretches forth his hand for water to reach his mouth, but it reaches him not."**

'Ali bin Abi Talib pictured it as a man stretching his hand on the edge of a deep well to reach the water: "even though his hands do not reach it; so how can the water reach his mouth?" Mujahid pictured something even more desperate — a man **calling the water with his words and pointing at it**, "but it will never come to him this way." Ibn Kathir draws the meaning out: he who stretches his hand towards water from far away, to either collect some or draw some, will not benefit from that water, which never reaches his mouth — where water is meant to be consumed. Likewise, Ibn Kathir says, those who call on another deity besides Allah will never benefit from these deities — **not in this life, and not in the Hereafter.**

Feel how carefully the parable is built. The thirst is real. The effort is real. The water is real. The only thing missing is any connection between the reaching and the water — and so the whole performance is motion without result. Hence the verdict: **"and the invocation of the disbelievers is nothing but misguidance."**

And set that beside ayah 12. There, water is lifted from the surface of the sea, carried through the atmosphere to places near and far, and poured out on lands Allah chooses — without anyone reaching for it. Here, a man strains for a mouthful and gets nothing. The difference is not effort. It is Who is being asked.

## Everything is already prostrating

**"And unto Allah falls in prostration whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly or unwillingly, and so do their shadows in the mornings and in the afternoons."**

Ibn Kathir reads this as Allah affirming His might and power: He has full control over everything, and everything is subservient to Him. Therefore everything prostrates to Allah — **the believers willingly, the disbelievers unwillingly.** This is the answer to the disputing in ayah 13. The disputer imagines his argument gives him some independence. It does not; nothing is outside Allah's control, and the bolt falls when Allah wills. Submission is not optional in this universe. Only *willing* submission is.

Then the detail that makes the ayah unforgettable: **"and so do their shadows in the mornings and in the afternoons."** Ibn Kathir glosses *bil-ghuduwwi* as the beginning of the days and *al-āṣāl* as towards the end of the days. Watch a shadow early in the day — long, stretched, laid flat along the ground — and again as the day closes and it leans the other way. Even the shadow you cast, which you did not make and cannot control, is doing this on a schedule Allah set. Ibn Kathir places another ayah alongside it: *"Have they not observed things that Allah has created: (how) their shadows incline"* (16:48).

## Living it

The passage asks three concrete things of a believer.

**Read the weather as speech.** Thunder is *tasbīh*; lightning, in the narration Ibn Kathir cites, is the smile of a cloud; and the bolt falls upon whom Allah wills. When the storm comes, say what the Prophet ﷺ used to say: *"O Allah! Do not kill us with Your anger, nor destroy us with Your torment, and save us before that."* Better still, do as Ibn Az-Zubayr did — stop talking altogether and praise the One Whom the thunder praises.

**Hold fear and hope together.** Qatadah's traveller and resident are looking at the same sky. A believer carries both readings at once: fear of the punishment that struck Arbad, and hope in the rain Allah lifts from the sea and delivers over the lands He chooses.

**Check where your calls are going.** *Lahu daʿwat al-ḥaqq* — every request placed anywhere but with Allah is a hand stretched towards water that never reaches the mouth. And ayah 15 removes the last excuse: you are going to prostrate either way. The only real choice left is whether you do it willingly.

passages.title: Who is the Lord? The rain parable
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat move from a question, to a picture, to a verdict — and one theme runs through all of them: **what lasts, and what only looks impressive for a while.** In ayah 16 the Prophet ﷺ is told to put a question to the idolaters and then to answer it himself, because they already hold the answer. In ayah 17 Allah draws two pictures from ordinary working life — rain running down a valley, and metal melting in a furnace — to show what happens when truth and falsehood are left side by side. In ayah 18 comes the verdict: two responses, two endings.

## "Say: Allah" — the question that answers itself

Ibn Kathir explains why this argument works: the people being questioned already hold the answer inside their own creed. They admit that Allah alone created the heavens and the earth, that He is their Lord and the Disposer of all affairs. That is why the verse does not wait for a reply. The question is asked and answered in the same breath — *"Say: Who is the Lord of the heavens and the earth? Say: Allah."* It is not asking for information they lack; it is holding up something they have already conceded.

Then the follow-up lands: *"Have you then taken awliyā' — protectors — other than Him, such as have no power either for benefit or for harm to themselves?"* Ibn Kathir spells out the reach of that phrase: these false gods have no power to benefit or harm themselves, nor those who worship them. And so his conclusion follows — the idolaters will get no benefit from these false deities, and no harm will be lifted from them by these deities either.

**The blind and the seeing, darkness and light.** Ibn Kathir reads this pair as a comparison of two kinds of worshipper: are those who worship false deities instead of Allah equal to those who worship Him alone, without partners? Notice what he attaches to the second group — those who worship Him alone "and thus have a light from their Lord." The comparison is not between two opinions of equal standing. One side is described in the language of sight; the other in the language of blindness.

**"Or do they assign to Allah partners who created the like of His creation, so that the creation seemed alike to them?"** Ibn Kathir unpacks the challenge: have their so-called gods produced a rival creation alongside Allah's, so that the two got mixed up and they honestly cannot tell whose is whose? The very asking of it shows the answer. Rather, says Ibn Kathir, the ayah proves that the truth is nothing like this. There is none similar to Allah — no equal, no rival, no one like Him, no minister, no son, no wife. Allah is glorified far above everything ascribed to Him.

**They knew, and worshipped them anyway.** Ibn Kathir presses the point that the idols they served were ones they themselves admitted Allah had created and which were subservient to Him. He quotes the words they used in their own Talbiyah, the pilgrimage chant: *"Here we rush to Your obedience. There is no partner for You, except Your partner, You own him and he owns not."* Their stated defence appears elsewhere in the Qur'an — *"We worship them only that they may bring us near to Allah"* (39:3). Ibn Kathir answers it from the Qur'an itself: only those Allah chooses are permitted to intercede with Him — *"Intercession with Him profits not except for him whom He permits"* (34:23); and *"There is none in the heavens and the earth but comes unto the Most Gracious as a servant... and every one of them will come to Him alone on the Day of Resurrection"* (19:93–95).

That is the hinge of his argument: if all are Allah's servants, why should any of them worship each other — and on what proof? Ibn Kathir says they had none. They relied on sheer opinion and on innovation in the religion, while Allah had sent all of His Prophets and Messengers, from beginning to end, forbidding exactly this and ordering that none be worshipped besides Allah. They defied their Messengers and rebelled against them, and so the word of punishment struck them as a worthy recompense — *"And your Lord treats no one with injustice"* (18:49).

The ayah then closes not with more argument but by naming Him: *"Allah is the Creator of all things; and He is the One, the Irresistible."* Ibn Kathir's whole case rests on that first clause — they concede the creating, and worship follows from it.

## Rain down a valley, ore in a furnace

Ibn Kathir says this single ayah contains **two parables, both affirming that truth remains and increases, while falsehood diminishes and perishes.**

**The first parable — water.** *"He sends down water from the sky, and the valleys flow according to their measure."* Ibn Kathir: each valley takes its share according to its capacity, for some valleys are wider and can retain more water than others, which are small and retain less. And then he turns the picture inward: **this ayah indicates that hearts differ.** Some of them can retain substantial knowledge, while others cannot entertain knowledge at all but are actually bothered by it. What varies in the parable is not the rain; it is the valley.

*"But the flood bears away the foam that mounts up to the surface."* The foam rides on top of the very water that carries it — prominent, and on the surface.

**The second parable — fire.** *"And from that ore which they heat in the fire in order to make ornaments or utensils, rises a foam like unto it."* Ibn Kathir: gold and silver ore is heated with fire to make adornments, and iron and copper ore is heated to make pots and the like — and foam rises to the surface of these ores just as it does with water. Two completely different processes, water and fire, producing the same phenomenon.

*"Thus does Allah show forth truth and falsehood."* Ibn Kathir: when the two exist together, falsehood does not remain, just as foam does not remain with the water, or with the gold and silver ores heated in fire. Rather, it dissipates and vanishes. On *"as for the foam, it passes away as scum upon the banks,"* he notes that it carries no benefit at all: it scatters on the banks of the valley, sticks to the trees, or is dissipated by the wind — and the same is true of the scum that rises on gold, silver, iron and copper. It all goes away and never returns. However, water, gold and silver remain, and are used to man's benefit.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Tafsīr al-Jalālayn, states the outcome of both parables plainly: foam does appear prominent for a while on the real thing, but it finally gets thrown away and the real thing remains. Similar is the case of the false — though it may for a short while appear to have overcome the true, it is finally subdued and eliminated, and that which is true remains and stands manifestly proven. For a believer watching falsehood look large and confident in his own lifetime, that is the passage's consolation: **you are looking at foam, and foam is on the surface and on its way out.**

## Ibn ʿAbbās: the foam is doubt

There is a second reading, reported by ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭalḥah from ʿAbdullāh bin ʿAbbās, that takes the parable inside a person. He said: "This is a parable that Allah has set; the hearts carry knowledge from Him, and certainty according to the amount of doubt." On his reading, the foam that is swept away is **doubt**, and what stays in the ground and benefits people is **certainty**. And he adds a sharp line about each: as for doubt, working good deeds does not benefit while it exists; as for certainty, Allah benefits its people by it. Then he ties in the second parable — just as jewellery heated in fire is rid of its impurity, which remains in the fire, so Allah accepts certainty and discards doubt.

Read this way, the ayah is not only about the fortunes of truth and falsehood in the world. It is also about what a heart is carrying, and which part of that will still be there at the end.

**Parables demand work.** Ibn Kathir attaches to this the ayah *"And these similitudes We put forward for mankind; but none will understand them except those who have knowledge"* (29:43), and quotes some of the Salaf — the early generations — as saying: "When I would read a parable in the Qur'an that I could not comprehend, I would cry for myself," because of that verse. The parables of the Qur'an are not decoration to be skimmed; failing to grasp one was, for them, a cause for grief.

## Parables that use water and fire

Ibn Kathir observes that the Qur'an and the Sunnah both teach with water and with fire, and he lines up the parallels: the two parables of the hypocrites at the start of Sūrat al-Baqarah, one of a kindled fire (2:17) and one of a rainstorm bringing darkness, thunder and lightning (2:19); and the two parables for the disbelievers in Sūrat an-Nūr, the mirage (24:39) and the darkness of a vast deep sea (24:40).

**The water hadith.** It is recorded in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs that Abu Musa al-Ashʿarī said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that the example of the guidance and knowledge with which Allah has sent him is like abundant rain falling on the earth. Some of it was fertile soil that absorbed the rain water and brought forth vegetation and grass in abundance. Another portion was hard: it held the rain water, and Allah benefited the people with it — they drank, grazed, watered their animals and irrigated with it. And another portion fell on barren land, which could neither hold the water nor bring forth vegetation. The Prophet ﷺ then gave the meaning: the first is the example of the person who comprehends Allah's religion and gets benefit, as well as benefiting others from the knowledge and guidance Allah has revealed through him ﷺ, and who learns and then teaches others. The last is the example of the person who does not care for it and does not embrace Allah's guidance revealed through him ﷺ.

Ibn Kathir cites this as a parable that uses water — and placed next to ayah 17, the two speak the same language. *Valleys flow according to their measure*, and soils receive the same rain according to what they are. The revelation is one; the ground it lands on is not.

**The fire hadith.** Ibn Kathir also cites a narration collected by Imam Ahmad, in which Abu Hurayrah narrated that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ compared himself and his people to a man who lit a fire: when it illuminated his surroundings, butterflies and insects started falling into it, and he began swatting at them to prevent them from falling, but they overwhelmed him and kept falling in. Then he ﷺ said that this is the parable of him and them — "I am holding you by the waist trying to save you from the Fire, saying, 'Go away from the Fire,' yet you overwhelm me and fall into it." Ibn Kathir adds that the Two Ṣaḥīḥs also collected this hadith. It is worth pausing on what that image shows about him ﷺ: a man physically holding people back by the waist from something they are rushing into.

## Two answers, two endings

*"For those who answered their Lord's call is al-Ḥusnā."* Ibn Kathir defines what answering means concretely: they obeyed Allah and followed His Messenger ﷺ — obeying his commands, and believing the reports he brought about the past and the future. Both halves matter: acting on what he ﷺ instructed, and accepting what he ﷺ told us about what we cannot see.

**Al-Ḥusnā** is the good reward. Ibn Kathir illustrates it with Dhul-Qarnayn's words — *"as for him who believes and works righteousness, he shall have the best reward (al-Ḥusnā), and we shall speak unto him mild words by our command"* (18:87–88) — and with *"For those who have done good is the best (al-Ḥusnā) and even more"* (10:26). That last phrase is worth noticing: *and even more.* The good reward is not the end of it.

Then the other side. *"But those who answered not His call"* — that is, disobeyed Allah — *"if they had all that is in the earth together with its like, they would offer it in order to save themselves."* Ibn Kathir places this in the Hereafter: had such a person the earth's fill of gold and its like with it, he would try to ransom himself from Allah's torment at that moment. However, this will not be accepted from him; Allah the Exalted will not accept any type of exchange. Everything a person spends a life accumulating is, at the one moment it would matter most, worth nothing.

*"For them there will be the terrible reckoning."* Ibn Kathir explains this as being reckoned in the Hereafter for **the naqīr and the qiṭmīr** — the big and the small alike. And he draws out the principle: verily, he who is reckoned in detail on that Day will receive punishment.
