Hence what comes next: *"Their dwelling place will be Hell; and worst indeed is that place for rest."* The verse calls Hell a place of rest, and then calls it the worst of them.

## Living it

- **Widen the valley.** Ibn Kathir's reading of *"according to their measure"* puts the difference in the receptacle, not in the rain: hearts differ, and some can hold substantial knowledge while others are bothered by it. That is the diagnostic question to turn on yourself — not whether the knowledge reached you, but what it met when it arrived.
- **Doubt and certainty.** On Ibn ʿAbbās's reading the whole parable is about these two. Doubt is the foam that is swept away; certainty is what stays in the ground and benefits people. And his warning is blunt: while doubt exists, working good deeds does not benefit — whereas by certainty, Allah benefits its people. Allah accepts certainty and discards doubt.
- **Do not be impressed by foam.** Both Ibn Kathir and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān make the same point: falsehood may be prominent for a while on top of the real thing, but it is finally thrown away, and the real thing remains. Judge by what stays in the ground, not by what rides on top of the flood.
- **Answer the call.** Ayah 18 makes the whole thing turn on one act — responding to your Lord. And ayah 16 has already removed the excuse for not doing so: you already know who your Lord is.

passages.title: Covenant-keepers, their Gardens, and covenant-breakers
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** These seven ayat divide humanity in two and describe each side by its character rather than its label: the people who keep what they promised Allah, and the people who break it. Ayah 19 asks the question; ayat 20–22 list the marks of the covenant-keepers; ayat 23–24 show them arriving home, greeted by angels; ayah 25 turns every one of those clauses inside out. The word that stitches it together is *ʿahd* — pledge — kept in ayah 20, broken in ayah 25.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān places it precisely: the verses just before used **parables** to separate truth from falsehood, and ayah 18 stated the good return for the obedient and the severe punishment for the rest. Now the Qur'an moves from images to people.

## Ayah 19: the sighted and the blind

"Is the one who knows that what has been revealed to you from your Lord is the truth like the one who is blind?"

Ibn Kathir unpacks what such a person *knows*: that the revelation is the truth about which there is no doubt, in which there is no confusion, vagueness or contradiction — every part of it testifying to another, all its information true and all its commands and prohibitions just. He brings "And the Word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and in justice" (6:115): accurate in what it reports, just in what it orders.

The one contrasted with him is *aʿmā*, blind — not merely someone who disagrees. Ibn Kathir: he cannot find guidance to what would benefit him, cannot even comprehend it, and even if he does, he will not follow it, believe in it, or abide by it. The question is rhetorical; Ibn Kathir answers it from elsewhere: "Not equal are the dwellers of the Fire and the dwellers of Paradise" (59:20).

Then the close: **"But it is only the men of understanding who pay heed"** — *ūlū l-albāb*. Ibn Kathir: those with sound minds are the ones who draw lessons, gain wisdom and understand; he adds a du'a that Allah make us among them. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sharpens it: the comparison is obvious, yet only someone whose essential reason is still intact can appreciate it. Whoever has ruined that faculty through heedlessness and disobedience cannot see a difference this great. The problem is rarely the evidence; it is the eye.

## Ayat 20–22: nine marks of the people of the covenant

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān counts nine attributes in these three ayat. Ibn Kathir gathers them under one heading: these are the qualities of the blessed ones, who will earn the good final home — victory and triumph in this life and the Hereafter.

**1–2. "Those who fulfil Allah's covenant and do not break the pledge" (ayah 20).** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that *ʿahd Allah* covers every pledge Allah has taken from His servants — the very first being the covenant taken in eternity, before the assembly of all spirits: *alastu bi-rabbikum*, "Am I not your Lord?", to which all answered *balā*, "Yes — surely You are our Lord." It also covers the pledges throughout the Qur'an about obeying His injunctions, fulfilling assigned duties, and abstaining from what He forbade.

The second phrase, *wa lā yanquḍūna l-mīthāq*, widens the circle: it includes those pledges between Allah and His servants, the pledges a religious community gives its prophet, **and the contracts and pacts one human being makes with another**. Ibn Kathir draws the contrast ayah 25 will make explicit: such people are nothing like the hypocrites, who break covenants once made, quarrel bitterly, lie when they speak, and betray a trust.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then gives the passage its most memorable illustration. Abu Dawud reports, on the narration of Sayyidna ʿAwf ibn Malik, that the Prophet ﷺ took a pledge from the noble Ṣaḥābah that they would not associate anyone with Allah, would perform Salah punctually five times a day, would obey their authorities, and **would never stretch out their hands to any human being for anything**. Those who gave that pledge held to it so exactly that if one dropped his whip while riding, he would not ask a bystander to hand it up — he would dismount and pick it up himself.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful here: the Prophet ﷺ plainly never intended to forbid a request that small. What it shows is the love and passion for obedience in their hearts. The commentary pairs it with Sayyidna ʿAbdullah ibn Masʿūd, walking into the Masjid when he heard the Prophet ﷺ, mid-address, say "Sit down." He knew the instruction was not aimed at people out on the street — yet his passion for obedience would not let him take one more step. He sat down where he stood, at the gate.

**3. "Those who join what Allah has commanded to be joined" (ayah 21).** Ibn Kathir: they are good to their relatives and do not sever the bond of kinship; they are kind to the poor and needy, and generous by nature. Beyond this well-known meaning, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, some explained it as joining righteous deeds to faith, or joining faith in the Prophet ﷺ and the Qur'an to faith in the earlier prophets and their books.

**4. "And they fear their Lord" — *wa yakhshawna rabbahum*.** Here Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens up the Arabic. The word is *khashyah*, not *khawf*. *Khawf* is the fear you feel facing a beast or a dangerous man. *Khashyah* is closer to the fear a child has of a parent, or a student of a teacher — no dread of being harmed, but an apprehension born of love and esteem, that something you say or do might displease the one you honour. That is why, wherever fear of Allah appears in a context of praise, the word is generally *khashyah*.

**5. "And they dread the evil reckoning."** Precisely because this fifth quality concerns a reckoning that is strict and minute, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out, the word here is *not khashyah* but plain fear — *yakhāfūna sūʾa l-ḥisāb*. Sayyidah ʿĀʾishah said that Divine mercy alone can save a human being, when matters are forgiven summarily at the reckoning; anyone made to account for every single thing said and done cannot escape punishment. Who could claim never to have sinned? Ibn Kathir adds the daily effect of this fear: they remember that Allah is watching in everything they do and leave undone, so all their affairs run straight — especially those that affect others.

**6. "Those who are patient, seeking their Lord's Face" (ayah 22).** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān warns that *ṣabr* is much wider than "patience under distress." Its real meaning is that a person does not come apart under what is temperamentally unpalatable, and keeps doing what must be done, steadily. Hence its two branches: *ṣabr ʿalā al-ṭāʿah*, steadfastness in carrying out Allah's commands, and *ṣabr ʿalā al-maʿṣiyah*, steadfastness in staying away from sin. Ibn Kathir reads it the same way: patient in avoiding sins while devoting themselves to their Lord's service, seeking His pleasure and generous reward.

The qualifier *ibtighāʾa wajhi rabbihim* — seeking their Lord's Face — is doing heavy lifting. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: bare patience is no merit at all, since even the most impatient person eventually becomes reconciled to his lot, and Allah never obligates anyone with what is beyond his control. The Prophet ﷺ said that the real, trustworthy *ṣabr* is the one taken up **at the first shock**; later, one has no choice but to accept. The commentary presses it: a man breaks into a house to steal, finds no opportunity, and leaves. That "restraint" earns nothing. It earns reward only when a person abstains out of fear of Allah and desire for His pleasure.

**7. "And they establish the Salah."** Ibn Kathir: preserving its limits, its times, its bowing, its prostration and its humbleness, according to the established rulings of the religion. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the Qur'an uses *iqāmah* — "establishing" — rather than merely "saying" prayers: performing it with all its conditions, its etiquette, and the necessary humility of heart, not as routine.

**8. "And they spend from what We have provided them, secretly and openly."** Ibn Kathir: they spend on those they are obliged to support — spouses, relatives, the poor and needy — in all conditions, night or day. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the gentleness of *mimmā razaqnāhum*, "from what **We** have given them": Allah is not asking you for something of yours, but for a portion of what He gave you — and with Zakah, only two and a half percent.

The pairing "secretly and openly" also settles a practical question. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: concealment is not the only Sunnah way. Scholars have said obligatory charity — Zakah, Ṣadaqat al-Fiṭr — is better given openly, so others are prompted to do the same; voluntary charity is better given secretly, so one stays safe from hypocrisy and the pull of recognition. The ahadith praising secret giving concern this second, optional kind.

**9. "And they repel evil with good."** Ibn Kathir: they meet evil with good conduct — when people harm them, they face that harm with patience, forbearance, forgiveness and pardon. He cites: "Repel with that which is better, and then the one between whom and you there was enmity will become as though he were a close friend. But none is granted it except those who are patient, and none is granted it except the owner of a great portion" (41:34–35). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes it concrete: whoever wrongs you, deal with him justly; whoever denies your right, give him his; whoever unloads anger on you, answer with forbearance.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers a second reading: one repels one's *own* sin with obedience. The Prophet ﷺ told Sayyidna Muʿādh that if you do good after evil it will wipe out the evil, and Sayyidna Abu Dharr al-Ghifārī reported that the Prophet ﷺ said the same — when a sin happens, follow it up with a good deed that washes it off. The condition attached: the good deed must come after genuine shame and repentance — good works without repenting are not sufficient for that sin's forgiveness.

**The reward stated:** *ulāʾika lahum ʿuqbā l-dār* — "for them is the ultimate abode." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: *al-dār* refers to the Hereafter, so its success is theirs; though some commentators took it to include this world — good people face hardship here, but in the end it is they who come through.

## Ayat 23–24: what home looks like

**"Gardens of ʿAdn, which they will enter."** Ibn Kathir: *ʿAdn* indicates continuous residence — gardens of everlasting life. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: the root means to settle permanently, and no one will ever be expelled; some commentators said ʿAdn is the name of the midmost part of Paradise, the most superior of its stations.

**"Along with the righteous among their fathers, their spouses and their offspring."** Ibn Kathir: Allah will gather them with their loved ones — fathers, family, offspring — those righteous and deserving of Paradise, so that their eyes are comforted by seeing them. And He will raise those of lower rank to the level of those above them, as a favour from Him, **without lowering the rank of the higher**. He cites: "And those who believed and whose offspring followed them in faith — We will join their offspring to them" (52:21). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the condition and mechanism: the family must themselves be believers — the minimum being that they are Muslims, not disbelievers — and it is through the *barakah* of the accepted servant of Allah that relatives whose deeds fell short are raised to his station. Connection to the righteous, by lineage, kinship or friendship, benefits a person in the Hereafter — subject always to faith.

**"And the angels will enter upon them from every gate."** Ibn Kathir: they come from every direction to congratulate them, greeting them with the Islamic greeting and commending them for having earned Allah's closeness and reward, and admission to the Dwelling of Peace as neighbours of the honoured Messengers, the Prophets and the truthful believers.

Ibn Kathir then cites the hadith that gives this scene its faces. **Imam Ahmad recorded** that ʿAbdullah bin ʿAmr bin al-ʿĀṣ narrated that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ asked, "Do you know who among Allah's creation will enter Paradise first?" They said, "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said they are the **poor emigrants** — by whom the frontiers are secured and afflictions warded off, one of whom dies with his need still in his chest, unable to fulfil it. Allah will tell whichever angels He wills, "Go to them and greet them with Salām." The angels will say, "We are the dwellers of Your heaven and the best of Your creation — do You command us to go to *them* and greet them?" Allah will say, "They are My servants who worshipped Me and associated nothing with Me," repeating their description. So the angels come to them from every gate, saying: **"Peace be upon you for your patience — how excellent is the final home!"**

Notice what the angels name. Not wealth, not station — *ṣabr*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the lesson from ayah 24: the high ranks of Paradise are the outcome of a person's patient handling of this world's trials, insisting on the rights of Allah and of His servants and forcing the self away from disobedience. And the angels' word is *salām*: that patience has bought them permanent security from every hardship.

## Ayah 25: the same list, reversed

"And those who break Allah's covenant after its ratification, and sever what Allah has commanded to be joined, and spread corruption in the land — upon them is the curse, and theirs is the evil home."

Ibn Kathir: this is the destination of the wretched, and their characteristics are deliberately the mirror image of the believers' qualities just listed. He cites the report that the signs of a hypocrite are three — when he speaks he lies, when he promises he breaks it, when entrusted he betrays — and another wording adds treachery in covenants and foulness in dispute. *Al-laʿnah*, the curse, means they are cast away from Allah's mercy; *sūʾ al-dār* is the evil end and destination — "their dwelling place will be Hell, and worst indeed is that place of rest" (13:18).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān traces the three traits in order. **Breaking the pledge** includes the primordial pledge of Allah's oneness, which the polytheists broke on entering this world by attaching hundreds of lords to His pristine divinity; and it includes every obligation folded inside the Kalimah *lā ilāha illa Allāh, Muḥammadur rasūlullāh* — "There is no deity worthy of worship except Allah, Muhammad is the messenger of Allah" — so that deviating from any binding command of Allah or His Messenger ﷺ is a breach of that pledge of faith. **Severing what Allah joined** includes the relationship with Allah, His Messenger ﷺ and Allah's blessings — cutting it means contravening the commands — and it includes kinship: such people will not fulfil the rights of mother, father, brother, sister or neighbour. **Corruption in the land** is the *result* of the first two: once a person disregards pledges and has no regard for anyone's rights, his conduct brings pain and loss to others and becomes a cause of fighting and killing. And *laʿnah* — being far removed from Allah's mercy — is the most punishing of all punishments.

## Living it

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws two rulings straight out of ayat 20–21. **Keeping a contract is binding and breaking it is ḥarām** in every case — whether the pledge is with Allah and His Messenger ﷺ, with a Muslim, or with a non-Muslim. And **Islam is not monasticism**: the rights of parents, children, wife, siblings, other relatives and neighbours are obligations Allah placed on every person, and cannot be set aside for voluntary worship — not even to free up time for religious service to the community.

The commentary's hadith on kinship are worth keeping close. In a hadith of **al-Bukhari and Muslim** from Sayyidna Anas, the Prophet ﷺ said that whoever hopes for extended means of living and barakah in what he does should maintain his family ties. In a narration of Sayyidna ʿAbdullah ibn ʿUmar appearing in the **Ṣaḥīḥ of al-Bukhari**, the Prophet ﷺ taught that *ṣilat al-raḥim* is not merely returning a relative's favour; the real thing is that even when your relative fails to keep the tie with you, you — for Allah's sake alone — keep it with him and do him good. **Tirmidhi** reports that the Prophet ﷺ said, "Preserve your family trees," through which family ties are preserved and their rights can be fulfilled — and that keeping those ties generates mutual love and puts barakah in wealth and in years of life. In a hadith of **Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim**, the Prophet ﷺ said that the most commendable form of it is a man keeping up the same relations with his late father's friends as they were in his father's lifetime. And Sayyidna Abu Ayyub al-Ansari related that a bedouin villager called on the Prophet ﷺ at his home and asked what he should do to come closer to Paradise and stay away from the Fire; he ﷺ answered: worship Allah, take no partners with Him, establish Salah, give Zakah, and maintain the ties of kinship (**al-Baghawi**).

Read whole, the passage makes one point: the difference between the two destinations is not claimed belief but whether a person's word holds — with Allah, and with the people Allah placed in his life. May Allah keep us all from the fate described in ayah 25.

passages.title: Provision, guidance, and hearts at rest
passages.tafsir:
Ayat 26–29 are held together by a single question: what does a heart come to rest on? Ayah 26 shows people whose hearts have settled on worldly provision — which Allah alone measures out, wide for some and narrow for others. Ayah 27 shows those same people demanding a spectacular miracle before they will believe. Ayah 28 gives what neither wealth nor spectacle can give: hearts find their rest in the remembrance of Allah. And ayah 29 names what waits at the end of that road — *Ṭūbā*, and a beautiful place of return.

Ibn Kathir marks the movement with his own section headings across these four ayat: "Increase and Decrease in Provision is in Allah's Hand," then "Disbelievers ask for Miracles, Allah's Response to Them," then "The Believer's Heart finds Comfort in the Remembrance of Allah," then "The Meaning of Tuba." Read in order, those four headings trace one arc — from what people lean on, to what they demand, to what actually holds a heart, to what that heart ends in.

## Ayah 26 — Provision is opened and closed by Allah alone

**"Allah gives abundant or limited provisions to whoever He wills."** Ibn Kathir states the meaning plainly: Allah alone increases the provisions for whom He wills and decreases it for whom He wills, "according to His wisdom and perfect justice."

Two things follow from that, and the ayah makes both.

**A wide provision is not a certificate of Allah's approval.** Ibn Kathir writes that when the disbelievers rejoice with the life of the present world that was given to them, "they do not know that they are being tested and tried." He brings a verse that says it outright: *"Do they think that in wealth and children with which We enlarge them, We hasten unto them with good things? Nay, but they perceive not"* (23:55–56). Wealth arriving is not the same as good arriving. It may be the test itself.

Notice, too, that both halves of the sentence are His act. Ibn Kathir renders the pair as He "increases the provision for whom He wills, and straitens (it for whom He wills)" — the widening and the narrowing named in one breath, as one wisdom. The one whose provision is narrow is no more outside His decree than the one whose provision is wide.

**And the rejoicing is misplaced because the thing rejoiced in is small.** The ayah says *"they rejoice in the life of the world"* and then immediately cuts it down to size: *"whereas the life of this world compared to the Hereafter is but a brief passing enjoyment."* Ibn Kathir's own comment on that phrase is that here "Allah belittled the life of the present world in comparison to what He has prepared for His believing servants in the Hereafter." He gathers other ayat to the same effect: *"Say: 'Short is the enjoyment of this world. The Hereafter is (far) better for him who has Taqwa'"* (4:77) — *Taqwa* being that watchful consciousness of Allah that keeps a person within His limits — and *"Nay, you prefer the life of this world, although the Hereafter is better and more lasting"* (87:16–17).

**From the Sunnah.** Imam Ahmad recorded that Al-Mustawrid, from Banī Fihr, said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"The life of the present world, compared to the Hereafter, is just like when one of you inserts his finger in the sea, so let him contemplate how much of it will it carry"* — and he pointed with the index finger. Imam Muslim also collected this hadith in his Ṣaḥīḥ.

Sit with the image. The point is not that the drop on the finger is nothing; it is wet, it is real, it is genuinely from the sea. The point is the sea. A person who has arranged his whole life around what fits on a fingertip has not made an evil calculation so much as an absurdly small one.

Ibn Kathir follows it with what he introduces only as "another Hadith" — without naming any collection, so we leave the attribution exactly where he left it. The Prophet ﷺ passed by a dead sheep whose ears were small, and said: *"By Allah! The life of this present world is as insignificant to Allah as this sheep was to its owners when they threw it away."*

## Ayah 27 — "Why is no sign sent down to him?"

Ayah 27 moves from what the disbelievers *enjoy* to what they *demand*: **"And those who disbelieved say: 'Why is not a sign sent down to him from his Lord?'"** Ibn Kathir notes they said the same elsewhere — *"Let him then bring us an Ayah like the ones (Prophets) that were sent before (with signs)!"* (21:5). (*Ayah* here means a sign or miracle, the same word the Qurʼan uses for its own verses.) Ibn Kathir adds that Allah "is able to bring them what they wanted." The issue was never capability.

### The moment behind the demand

This is the most illuminating thing in the passage, and Ibn Kathir introduces it simply as "a Hadith" — without naming its collection, so we will not name one either.

The idolaters asked the Prophet ﷺ to turn Mount aṣ-Ṣafā into gold. They asked him for a spring to gush forth for them. They asked that the mountains around Makkah be removed and replaced with green fields and gardens. And Allah revealed to His Messenger ﷺ: *"If You wish, O Muhammad, I will give them what they asked for. However, if they disbelieve thereafter, I will punish them with a punishment that I did not punish any among the ʿĀlamīn"* — mankind and the jinn — *"Or, if you wish, I will open for them the door to repentance and mercy."*

The Prophet ﷺ said: **"Rather, open for them the door to repentance and mercy."**

Understand what he ﷺ turned down. Total vindication: the mountain turned to gold in front of the very people refusing to believe him, and if they still refused, a punishment unlike any inflicted on anyone before them. When that door was held open for him, he asked instead that a different door be opened — for *them*.

Ibn Kathir then says: **"This is why Allah said to His Messenger ﷺ next,"** and gives the rest of the ayah. The connection is the whole point. The verse does not answer the demand for a sign with a sign. It answers with the mechanism of guidance itself.

### Why the miracle would not have worked anyway

**"Say: 'Verily, Allah sends astray whom He wills and guides unto Himself those who turn to Him in repentance.'"** Ibn Kathir's comment: Allah brings misguidance or guidance whether the Messenger ﷺ was given a sign according to their asking or not — "earning the misguidance or the guidance are not connected to the miracles or the lack of them." He supports this with a striking run of ayat: *"But neither Ayat nor warners benefit those who believe not"* (10:101); *"Truly, those, against whom the Word of your Lord has been justified, will not believe. Even if every sign should come to them, until they see the painful torment"* (10:96–97); and most vividly, *"And even if We had sent down unto them angels, and the dead had spoken unto them, and We had gathered together all things before their very eyes, they would not have believed, unless Allah willed, but most of them behave ignorantly"* (6:111).

That last verse is worth reading slowly. Angels descending, the dead speaking, everything gathered before their eyes — and still no belief, "unless Allah willed." Evidence alone does not turn a will that has already refused. The demand "show me a sign" is often not a request for information at all.

**And who is guided?** The ayah names them: *"those who turn to Him in repentance"* — in Arabic, *man anāb*, the one who turns back. Ibn Kathir unpacks it: "He guides to Him those who repent, turn to Him, beg Him, seek His help and humbly submit to Him."

Hold the two halves of ayah 27 together as the ayah itself does. Allah sends astray whom He wills — His will is absolute and He is not answerable to His creation. And He guides to Himself the one who turns back — so the door is described, and its threshold is not cleverness or a miracle witnessed, but the posture Ibn Kathir lists: repenting, turning, begging, seeking His help, humbly submitting. The Prophet ﷺ had just asked that the door of repentance be opened; the ayah tells us exactly who walks through it.

## Ayah 28 — The heart that finds its rest

**"Those who believed, and whose hearts find rest in the remembrance of Allah."** Ibn Kathir: "their hearts find comfort on the side of Allah, become tranquil when He is remembered and pleased to have Him as their Protector and Supporter."

Now put ayah 28 beside ayah 26 and the shape of the whole passage appears. In ayah 26 the disbelievers *rejoice* in the life of this world. In ayah 28 the believers' hearts *find rest* in the remembrance of Allah. These are two different states, not two intensities of one state. Rejoicing rides on circumstances; when the provision widens it rises, and when the provision narrows it collapses. The word the ayah uses of the believers is *taṭmaʼinn* — rendered "find rest," and glossed by Ibn Kathir as finding comfort and becoming tranquil. It is a heart that has stopped casting about, because it has found what it was looking for.

Then the ayah restates itself in a wider form: **"Verily, in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest."** The first half described a particular people — *their* hearts. The second half drops the possessive and speaks of hearts as such. And Ibn Kathir closes his comment with a line worth memorising: "and surely, He is worthy of it." The heart does not rest in the remembrance of Allah because of some psychological trick. It rests there because He is genuinely the One worth resting in.

There is a quiet mercy in the placement, too. Ayah 27 has just said that Allah sends astray whom He wills — a statement that can unsettle a sincere reader. Ayah 28 immediately shows what a guided heart *feels like* from the inside, and it is not anxiety. The one who finds himself settled by the remembrance of Allah is being shown something about where he stands.

## Ayah 29 — Ṭūbā, and a beautiful return

**"Those who believed, and work righteousness, Ṭūbā is for them and a beautiful place of (final) return."** Note that ayah 29 adds the limb ayah 28 left out: belief that rests in Allah's remembrance and then *works*. Inward stillness and outward action are one life, not two.

### What Ṭūbā means

Ibn Kathir gathers the early authorities, and the range is itself instructive:

- **Ibn ʿAbbās** (reported by ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭalḥah): "Happiness and comfort or refreshment of the eye."
- **ʿIkrimah**: "How excellent is what they earned."
- **Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk**: "A joy for them."
- **Ibrāhīm An-Nakhʿī**: "Better for them."
- **Qatādah**: it is an Arabic word that means "you have earned a good thing"; in another narration from him, "It is excellent for them."

Ibn Kathir's verdict on the spread: "These meanings for Ṭūbā are all synonymous and they do not contradict one another." That is a useful lesson in how to read tafsir. Not every difference between the early authorities is a dispute. Here they are five people circling one untranslatable word — goodness, gladness, the eye at rest, a good thing well earned — and each has caught a real facet of it.

### Ṭūbā as a tree, and a triple share for us

Imam Ahmad recorded that Abū Saʿīd Al-Khudrī said that a man asked, "O Allah's Messenger! Ṭūbā for those who saw you and believed in you!" The Prophet ﷺ said: **"Ṭūbā is for he who saw me and believed in me. Ṭūbā, and another Ṭūbā, and another Ṭūbā for he who believed in me, but did not see me."**

Read that again as someone who never saw him ﷺ. The questioner names the ones with the obvious privilege — and the Prophet ﷺ says it three times over for those who came after, believing on report, without the face in front of them. The people demanding a sign in ayah 27 had the Messenger ﷺ standing before them and refused; and here, those who never saw and still believed are given a threefold share.

Then a man asked, "What is Ṭūbā?" The Prophet ﷺ said: **"A tree in Paradise whose width is a hundred years, and the clothes of the people of Paradise are taken from its bark."** Al-Bukhārī and Muslim recorded that Sahl bin Saʿd said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: **"There is a tree in Paradise, if a rider travels in its shade for one hundred years, he would not be able to cross it."** An-Nuʿmān bin Abī ʿAyyāsh Az-Zuraqī added that Abū Saʿīd Al-Khudrī narrated to him the version with a rider on "a fast, sleek horse" — a hundred years at speed, still in the shade.

Ibn Kathir also records a statement of Khālid bin Maʿddān — his own words, not attributed to the Prophet ﷺ, and Ibn Abī Ḥātim collected it — that there is a tree in Paradise called Ṭūbā which nurses the children of the people of Paradise.

And Ibn Kathir places here what Imam Muslim recorded in his Ṣaḥīḥ, that Abū Dharr narrated that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that Allah the Exalted and Most Honored said: **"O My slaves! If the first and the last among you, mankind and Jinns among you, stood in one spot and asked Me and I gave each person what he asked, it will not decrease from My dominion, except what the needle decreases (or carries) when entered into the sea."** The sea has returned, and the comparison has flipped. In ayah 26 our whole world was the drop clinging to a finger. Here every request of every creature who ever lived is what a needle takes from the sea. So ask. Nothing you ask for diminishes Him.

The ayah ends **"and a beautiful place of (final) return"** — which Ibn Kathir glosses as the final destination. Ṭūbā is what they have; the beautiful return is where they end.

## Living it

- **Read your bank balance as a test, not a verdict** (ayah 26). Ibn Kathir's warning is that the people rejoicing in what they were given "do not know that they are being tested and tried." Wide or narrow, it came by His wisdom and perfect justice — and it is a fingertip's worth of sea either way.
- **Stop waiting for a sign** (ayah 27). Guidance was never contingent on spectacle — "neither Ayat nor warners benefit those who believe not." What is asked of you is what Ibn Kathir lists: to repent, turn to Him, beg Him, seek His help, humbly submit. The Prophet ﷺ asked for that door to be held open. Walk through it.
- **Treat the remembrance of Allah as the actual remedy for an unsettled heart** (ayah 28), not as a consolation prize after the real solutions fail. The ayah states it of hearts as such, and Ibn Kathir gives the reason: He is worthy of it.
- **Let the stillness produce work** (ayah 29). Ṭūbā is promised to those who believed *and* work righteousness.
- **When you feel the distance of never having seen him ﷺ**, remember: Ṭūbā, and another Ṭūbā, and another Ṭūbā.

passages.title: A denying people, and messengers mocked before you
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** The Makkan leaders came to the Prophet ﷺ with a bargain: make your Qur'an move the mountains, fold up the distances, bring our dead ancestor back to speak — and we will believe. These three ayat are the answer. Ayah 30 places the Prophet's ﷺ mission inside a long line of messengers sent to communities that denied them; ayah 31 refuses the staged miracle and points to the Qur'an itself as the greater sign, with all decision resting with Allah; ayah 32 comforts him ﷺ with what became of those who mocked the messengers before him. One thread runs through all three: rejection is not new, the Book itself is the miracle, and the outcome belongs to Allah alone.

The section just before had sorted people into two kinds — those who keep their pledge with Allah, and those who break it, sever what Allah commanded to be joined and spread corruption, whose portion is "the curse and the evil abode" (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān). Now the Qur'an turns to the Prophet ﷺ, who has to stand in front of exactly such people.

## "And so We have sent you" — ayah 30

Ibn Kathir reads the opening word *kadhālika* ("thus", "just so") as a comparison drawn across history: "Just as We sent you, O Muhammad, to your Ummah… Likewise, We sent others to earlier nations that disbelieved in Allah. The Messengers whom We sent before you, were also denied and rejected, so you have an example in what they faced." He cites Allah's words elsewhere, "By Allah, We indeed sent (Messengers) to the nations before you" (16:63), and "Verily, many Messengers were denied before you, with patience they bore the denial and suffering until Our help reached them" (6:34) — which Ibn Kathir glosses as a reminder of "how We gave them victory and granted the best end for them and their followers in this life and the Hereafter."

There is a warning folded into the comfort. Since Allah sent His punishment on those earlier deniers, Ibn Kathir has the ayah say: "then let these people fear what will strike them, for their denial of you is harsher than the denial that the previous Messengers faced."

**The job description.** The mission is defined by a purpose clause — *li-tatluwa ʿalayhim alladhī awḥaynā ilayk*, "in order that you might recite unto them what We have revealed to you." Ibn Kathir explains it simply: "so that you deliver to them Allah's Message." Note what he ﷺ is *not* told to do: produce wonders on demand. His assignment is recitation and delivery — precisely the point the next ayah will press.

## "While they disbelieve in Ar-Rahman"

The ayah does not merely say they disbelieve — it names the attribute they refuse. Ibn Kathir: "These people, that We sent you to, disbelieve in the Most Gracious and deny Him, because they dislike describing Allah by *Ar-Rahman Ar-Rahim* [the Most Gracious, Most Merciful]."

This was not theory. Ibn Kathir points to the day of Al-Hudaybiyyah, as narrated by Al-Bukhari, when the Quraysh refused to let the treaty be written with the words "In the Name of Allah, Ar-Rahman Ar-Rahim," saying, "We do not know Ar-Rahman Ar-Rahim!" (Qatadah narrated these words.) Their quarrel was with the mercy-name itself. And Allah's reply, in another ayah Ibn Kathir cites: "Say: Invoke Allah or invoke the Most Gracious, by whatever name you invoke Him, for to Him belong the Best Names" (17:110).

How beloved that name is to Allah appears in a hadith Ibn Kathir brings here: Imam Muslim recorded in his *Sahih* from ʿAbdullah bin ʿUmar that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "The most beloved names to Allah the Exalted are: ʿAbdullah and ʿAbdur-Rahman."

**The four-clause reply.** Against their rejection, the Prophet ﷺ is given a short, complete creed to say back to them. Ibn Kathir takes it clause by clause. *"He is my Lord"* and *"none has the right to be worshipped but He"* — "for I believe in Allah in Whom you disbelieve and affirm His Divinity and Lordship." *"In Him is my trust"* — "in all of my affairs." *"And to Him I turn"* (*wa ilayhi matāb*) — "to Him I return and repent, for He alone is worthy of all this and none else besides Him." Belief, worship, reliance, repentance: the whole relationship in one line, and it is what a believer says when a hostile crowd wants a spectacle instead.

## The demand at the Kaʿbah — the occasion of ayah 31

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains why this ayah has the shape it does, and it changes how you hear it. The proofs were already in front of the Makkans — the whole texture of the Prophet's ﷺ life, and his miracles, plainly visible. But Abu Jahl had declared that his clan stood in *competition* with Banu Hashim: how could they ever concede that the Messenger of Allah had to rise from among their rivals? They were not asking; they were manoeuvring.

Citing *Tafsir al-Baghawi*, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that the disbelievers of Makkah — Abu Jahl ibn Hisham and ʿAbdullah ibn Umayyah among them — gathered at the Baytullah and sat at its rear, sending ʿAbdullah ibn Umayyah to the Prophet ﷺ with an offer: fulfil our demands through your Qur'an, and we will all embrace Islam. Three demands:

1. **Move the mountains.** Makkah is hemmed in by mountains, with no room to farm or grow fruit — so push the mountains back and widen our land. And they argued from his own teaching: the mountains were made subject to Dawud (peace be upon him), glorifying Allah along with him — and you, they said, are no less than Dawud in Allah's sight.
2. **Subdue the wind.** As the wind was made subject to Sulayman (peace be upon him), collapsing great distances — do the same for us, so our trade journeys to Syria and Yemen become easy.
3. **Raise the dead.** As ʿIsa (peace be upon him) brought the dead to life, bring back our forefather Qusayy, so we can ask him whether this religion of the Arab prophet is true.

(Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites this from Mazhari, with reference to al-Baghawi, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Marduwayh.)

## The sentence that stops mid-air

Ayah 31 opens with "if" and then, startlingly, never states the consequence: "And if there had been a Qur'an with which mountains could be moved, or the earth could be cloven asunder, or the dead could be made to speak…" — and instead of finishing, it turns: "But the decision of all things is certainly with Allah."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that the missing answer-clause is understood from the situation: *lamā āmanū* — **they still would not have believed**. The same thought, it notes, is stated openly at another place in the Qur'an dealing with a similar subject (6:111). The silence here is itself the rebuke: their demand did not deserve a completed sentence.

**The three phrases, precisely.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the literal sense of each, and they map exactly onto the three demands: *suyyirat bihi'l-jibāl* — mountains moved from their places; *quṭṭiʿat bihi'l-arḍ* — long distances traversed in a short time (the earth "cut through"); *kullima bihi'l-mawtā* — speaking to the dead after they have been brought back to life.

**They had already seen more.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's answer is plain: they had already witnessed greater. The splitting of the moon at the hands of the Prophet ﷺ is more astonishing than mountains shifting; inert pebbles speaking in his blessed hands and glorifying Allah is a greater thing than a dead man made to talk; and the night journey to al-Masjid al-Aqsa, onward through the heavens and back to Makkah in a brief span, outstrips any subjugation of wind. They saw it with their own eyes and did not believe. So the demands were never a search for proof — they were "a device to gain time," and worse: if the demands went unmet, they could sneer that Allah — far be it from Him — has no control over such things; or that the request made by His Messenger ﷺ has no effect, being neither heard nor accepted by Allah, and that he is therefore no Messenger of Allah at all.

## "But the decision of all things is certainly with Allah"

This clause blocks that trap. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: all power, choice and control belong to Allah, so the demands going unfulfilled has nothing to do with any limit on His power. It is that He alone knows the wisdom by which this universe runs, and He knew the doggedness and ill intent behind the request — that even if every demand were granted, they would still not believe. Ibn Kathir states the principle at its widest: "whatever He wills, occurs and whatever He does not will, never occurs… he whom Allah misguides, will never find enlightenment and he whom Allah guides, will never be misled." Ibn ʿAbbas commented on this clause with a sentence worth sitting with: "He will only do what He wills and He decided that He will not do that." (Ibn Ishaq reported a chain for this, and Ibn Jarir At-Tabari agreed with it.)

## The Qur'an is the miracle they were standing in

Ibn Kathir reads the opening of ayah 31 as praise of the Qur'an, ranking it above every revealed Book before it, and offers two ways of taking it. First: if any Book among the earlier revealed Books could have moved mountains, split the earth, or made the dead speak in their graves, "it would have been this Qur'an and none else." Second: this Qur'an is the one *most worthy* to do such things, "because of its marvelous eloquence that defies the ability of mankind and the Jinns, even if all of them gather their forces together to invent something like it or even a Surah like it." And yet the idolaters reject it.

A note from Ibn Kathir supports the first reading: earlier Books may also be called "Qur'an", since this Qur'an is built upon them all. He cites the report of Imam Ahmad from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "Reciting was made easy for Dawud in that he used to order that his animal be prepared for him to ride and in the meantime he would read the entire Qur'an. He used to eat only from what his hand made." Al-Bukhari also collected this hadith — and the "Qur'an" in it, Ibn Kathir says, means the Zabur.

## "Have the believers not yet realised…"

The next clause turns from the deniers to the Muslims: *a-fa-lam yay'as alladhīna āmanū* — Ibn Kathir renders it "Have not then those who believed yet known… that had Allah willed, He could have guided all mankind?"; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives "Are the believers not aware…?" and explains the wording as *having not yet lost hope* in these particular people ever entering faith.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, reporting from Imam al-Baghawi, tells us what prompted it: when the Companions heard the Makkans' demands, they began to wish they *would* be granted — then all of Makkah would become Muslim and Islam would be strengthened. This ayah came down in response. Sincere as the wish was, it misread how Allah works: had He willed, He would have given all humanity a guidance leaving them no choice but to submit. His wisdom decided otherwise — that people should choose, and carry the weight of that choice.

And Ibn Kathir insists the sign they were wishing for was already there: "there is not a miracle or evidence more eloquent or effective on the heart and mind than this Qur'an. Had Allah revealed it to a mountain, you would see the mountain shake and humbled from fear of Allah." He cites what is recorded in the Sahih, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "Every Prophet was given (a miracle) the type of which would make (some) people believe. What I was given, however, is a revelation from Allah to me, and I hope that I will have the most following among them on the Day of Resurrection." Ibn Kathir draws the conclusion: every prophet's miracle ended with his death, but this Qur'an remains as evidence for all time — "the miracle of the Qur'an will never end, nor will it become old the more it is read, nor will scholars ever have enough of it." A moved mountain would have been a spectacle for one generation; the Qur'an is a standing sign for every generation, including ours.

## The disaster that keeps arriving

The ayah then states an ongoing consequence: "a disaster (*qāriʿah*) will not cease to strike those who disbelieved because of their deeds, or it settles close to their homes, until the promise of Allah comes to pass."

The commentators differ on the detail, and the sources report the difference rather than settling it. On *qāriʿah*: Ibn ʿAbbas, as reported by Al-ʿAwfi, said it is a torment descending on them from heaven; in another narration from him (via ʿIkrimah) it means affliction; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders it "disaster, hardship or calamity." On "or it settles close to their homes": Al-Hasan (narrated by Qatadah) took it as referring to the disaster itself landing nearby — and Ibn Kathir calls this "the apparent meaning here"; Ibn ʿAbbas (via Al-ʿAwfi), with similar reports from Mujahid and Qatadah, took it to mean the Messenger of Allah ﷺ camping near their territory and fighting them. On "until the promise of Allah comes to pass": these scholars said it means the conquest of Makkah, while Al-Hasan Al-Basri said it means the Day of Resurrection. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān leans to the conquest of Makkah — the promise Allah made His Prophet ﷺ — while allowing the Day of Judgement as a possible sense.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes how literally it came true for the Makkans: famine, men killed or captured at Badr and Uhud, one struck by lightning, another overtaken by some calamity — blow after blow until Makkah itself was opened. Ibn Kathir sets it alongside "And indeed We have destroyed towns round about you, and We have shown them the Ayat in various ways that they might return" (46:27). The clause closes with a guarantee, not a threat: "Certainly, Allah breaks not His promise" — Ibn Kathir: His promise to His Messengers to aid them and their followers in this life and the Hereafter, as in "So think not that Allah will fail to keep His promise to His Messengers" (14:47).

**Living it.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a striking lesson from "or it settles close to their homes": when calamity strikes near you rather than on you, that nearness carries a message — those living close by are meant to be warned, to look at what happened to others and correct themselves. What was punishment for one people can become mercy for their neighbours, if they take it seriously. He observes that we hear of floods, cyclones and earthquakes almost daily and treat them as bare events, whereas earlier generations would turn to Allah, repent, seek forgiveness and give charity — and see their difficulties lifted. To fix our eyes only on material causes, forgetting the Causer of all causes, is to react like those who do not believe.

## Ayah 32: respite is not reprieve

The final ayah is pure consolation. Ibn Kathir titles this passage "Comforting the Messenger of Allah ﷺ": "And indeed many Messengers were mocked at before you" — "so you have a good example in them." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same: what he ﷺ was facing, he was not facing alone; prophets before him were mocked precisely because their deniers were not seized the moment they committed their crime.

That delay is named: *fa-amlaytu lilladhīna kafarū* — "I granted respite to those who disbelieved," which Ibn Kathir explains as deferring their judgement "for a term appointed." Then *thumma akhadhtuhum* — "and finally I punished them," with encompassing punishment. And the ayah ends not with a statement but a question: *fa-kayfa kāna ʿiqāb* — "then how was My punishment?" Ibn Kathir brings the parallel: "And many a township did I give respite while it was given to wrongdoing. Then in the end I seized it. And to Me is the final return" (22:48).

The mistake the mockers made was to read Allah's patience as Allah's indifference. Ibn Kathir corrects it with a hadith recorded in the Two Sahihs, that the Prophet ﷺ said, "Verily, Allah gives respite to the unjust until when He seizes him, He never lets go of him" — after which he ﷺ recited, "Such is the punishment of your Lord when He seizes the population of towns while they are doing wrong. Verily, His punishment is painful, severe" (11:102). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the closing image: when they reached the limit, the seizure came, and it "left none of them active enough to go on with their confrontation."

**What the passage leaves in your hands.** Do not measure truth by whether the sky performs on demand — those who had seen the moon split still asked for one more sign. Do not measure Allah's judgement by the clock: delay is a term appointed, not a cancellation. And the believer's line is the one given to the Prophet ﷺ in ayah 30: "He is my Lord. None has the right to be worshipped but He. In Him is my trust, and to Him I turn."

passages.title: The Watcher over every soul, and the two ends
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** These three ayat set two things beside each other and let the contrast do the work. Ayah 33 asks whether the One who watches over every single soul, knowing all that it has earned, could seriously be placed on a level with lifeless idols — and then leaves the question unfinished, because no answer is needed. Ayah 34 states what awaits those who insist on the comparison. Ayah 35 answers from the other side with a description of the Garden. The unit closes on one word, *ʿuqbā* — rendered in our source as "the end (final destination)": this is where one road arrives, and that is where the other does.

## Ayah 33: a question deliberately left hanging

*A-fa-man huwa qāʾimun ʿalā kulli nafsin bimā kasabat* — "Is then He (Allah) Who takes charge of every person and knows all that he has earned?" And then the sentence breaks off and moves straight to "Yet, they ascribe partners to Allah." Ibn Kathir notes this explicitly: the answer to the question in the ayah was omitted, because it is implied. The Qurʼan will not dignify the comparison by completing it. You are meant to finish the sentence yourself — and to feel, while finishing it, how absurd the other side of it is.

**Watchful over everyone.** Ibn Kathir unpacks the phrase this way: Allah is the guard and watcher over every living soul, and knows what everyone does, whether good or evil, and nothing ever escapes His perfect observation. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders the same phrase "Is then He, who is watchful over everyone…" and supplies the other half of the idea — He is not merely the One who watches, but "the ultimate reckoner of everyone's deeds." So the phrase carries both senses at once: perfect watching, and a reckoning that follows from it.

**"Every person… all that he has earned."** The ayah does not speak of humanity in general. It speaks of every single soul, and links each one to what it has earned. Deeds are spoken of in the language of earnings: not things that happen and evaporate, but things a person acquires and carries.

**Ibn Kathir's chain of witnesses.** To show what this watching means, he lines up ayah after ayah from elsewhere in the Qurʼan:

- "Neither you do any deed nor recite any portion of the Qur'an… but we are witness thereof, when you are doing it" (10:61)
- "Not a leaf falls, but He knows it" (6:59)
- "And no moving creature is there on earth but its provision is due from Allah. And He knows its dwelling place and its deposits. All is in a Clear Book" (11:6)
- From this very surah: "It is the same (to Him) whether any of you conceals his speech or declares it openly, whether he be hid by night or goes forth freely by day" (13:10)
- "He knows the secret and that which is yet more hidden" (20:7)
- "And He is with you wherever you may be. And Allah is the All-Seer of what you do" (57:4)

Then he draws the conclusion the ayah left unspoken: is He Who is like this similar to the idols that the polytheists worship — which can neither hear nor see, nor do they have a mind, nor are they able to bring good to themselves or to their worshippers, nor prevent harm from themselves or their worshippers? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the same point bluntly: these people are certainly short on sense when they equate inert idols with His pure Being, a Being that watches everyone and is the ultimate reckoner of everyone's deeds.

## "Name them!"

*Qul sammūhum.* Ibn Kathir reads this as a challenge: make them known to us and uncover them so that they are known — for surely, they do not exist at all. Bring these deities out into the open and see whether anything is actually there.

The follow-up seals it: "Is it that you will inform Him of something He knows not in the earth?" Ibn Kathir's comment turns the whole ayah into a single closed argument — had that thing existed in or on the earth, Allah would have known about it, because nothing ever escapes His knowledge. The One who watches every soul obviously knows every so-called deity there is. So either you are informing Him of something real that He somehow missed — impossible, given how the ayah opened — or you are producing noise.

**"Or is it just a show of words?"** The early commentators read this phrase slightly differently. Mujahid understood it as doubts expressed in words; Ad-Dahhak and Qatadah said, false words. Either way it is talk with nothing underneath it. Ibn Kathir explains that the polytheists worshipped the idols because they thought that they had power to bring benefit or harm, and this is why they called them gods — and he brings the verdict of another ayah: "They are but names which you have named — you and your fathers — for which Allah has sent down no authority. They follow but a guess and that which they themselves desire, whereas there has surely come to them the guidance from their Lord!" (53:23)

## Why they could not see it

If the argument is that plain, why did it not land? The ayah answers: **"Nay! To those who disbelieved, their plotting is made fair-seeming."**

Mujahid glossed "their plotting" as their words. Ibn Kathir says this ayah refers to the misguidance of the polytheists and their propagation night and day — this was active work, not passive error. And he places beside it another ayah about how a thing comes to look attractive: "And We have assigned for them (devils) intimate companions, who have made fair-seeming to them" (41:25). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states the cause directly: shaitan has made their very ignorance look good in their sight, and therefore this they take to be "achievement" and "success."

This is the passage's sharpest psychological observation. They were not miserable in their falsehood. It looked attractive to them; it felt like winning. How something feels from the inside is no evidence at all that it is true.

**Two ways of reciting one word.** Ibn Kathir records both readings of the next phrase without choosing between them. Some read with Fatha over the Sad — *wa ṣaddū* — which would mean *they* hindered from the right path: being fond of the misguidance they are in, thinking that it is correct, they called others to it and thus hindered the people from following the path of the Messengers. Others read with Damma over the Sad — *wa ṣuddū* — which would mean *they have been* hindered from the right path: because they thought that their way looked fair or correct, they were hindered by it from the right path. Read the two together, as Ibn Kathir presents them, and a single picture emerges: the one who beautifies falsehood for others is walled off from guidance by the very wall he is building.

**"And whom Allah sends astray, for him there is no guide."** Ibn Kathir places two more ayat beside it: "And whomsoever Allah wants to suffer a trial, you can do nothing for him against Allah" (5:41), and "If you covet for their guidance, then verily, Allah guides not those whom He makes to go astray. And they will have no helpers" (16:37). Read that second one slowly, because it is a mercy for every believer who has exhausted himself over someone he loves. Even coveting another's guidance — wanting it fiercely, for years — cannot overturn the decree. The outcome was never yours to command, and you were never asked to command it.

## Ayah 34: the lighter punishment and the heavier one

Having described the Kufr and Shirk that the disbelievers indulge in, ayah 34 turns to consequence. Ibn Kathir understands "for them is a torment in the life of this world" as coming by the hands of the believers, killing and capturing them. Then, he says, comes the torment of the Hereafter — which will come after they suffer humiliation in this life — and it is *ashaqq*, harder: many times harder.

Ibn Kathir reports here that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to those who agreed to Mulāʿanah, "Surely, the torment of this life, is easier than the torment of the Hereafter." (Our source names no collection for this report, and tells us nothing further about the occasion.)

Ibn Kathir spells out why. The torment of this life ends, but the torment of the Hereafter is everlasting, in a Fire seventy times hotter than our fire, where there are chains whose thickness and hardness are unimaginable. He supports it with "So on that Day none will punish as He will punish. And none will bind as He will bind" (89:25–26), and with a longer passage on the Fire that "sees them from a far place" while "they will hear its raging and its roaring" — a passage that ends with exactly the turn our own passage is about to make: Say: "Is that (torment) better, or the Paradise of Eternity promised for those who have Taqwa?" It will be theirs as a reward and as a final destination (25:11–15).

**"And they have no defender (or protector) against Allah."** Ayah 34 closes off every avenue of rescue: there is no one to shield them from Him. That is the same point ayah 33 opened with, seen from the other side — He is the One who watches over every soul and reckons what it has earned, and there is none who can come between a soul and that reckoning.

## Ayah 35: the Garden described

Ayah 35 opens with *mathal al-jannah* — often translated "the parable of Paradise," but Ibn Kathir reads it plainly: it means its description and qualities. This is not a figure of speech standing in for something else. It is a report.

**"Underneath it rivers flow."** Ibn Kathir gives a detail easy to miss: these rivers flow in the various parts and grades of Paradise, and wherever its people wish they flow and gush forth for them. The water goes where the heart goes. He recalls the fuller description elsewhere: "The description of Paradise which those who have Taqwa have been promised (is that) in it are rivers of water the taste and smell of which are not changed, rivers of wine delicious to those who drink, and rivers of clarified honey, therein for them is every kind of fruit, and forgiveness" (47:15) — and note that last word, sitting among the rivers as though it were one of them.

**"Its provision is eternal, and so is its shade."** These are the two things this world can never manage. Food runs out; shade moves. Ibn Kathir: Paradise has foods, fruits and drinks that never end or finish, and the shade of Paradise is everlasting and never shrinks — as in "And fruit in plenty, whose supply is not cut off nor are they out of reach" (56:32–33), "And the shade thereof is close upon them, and the bunches of fruit thereof will hang low within their reach" (76:14), and "We shall admit them to shades wide and ever deepening" (4:57).

**From the Sunnah,** as Ibn Kathir cites it here:

- It is recorded in the Two Sahihs that Ibn ʿAbbas narrated, in the Hadith about the Eclipse prayer, that the Companions said, "O Allah's Messenger! While you were standing [in prayer], we saw you reach for something with your hand and then you brought it back." The Messenger ﷺ said: "I saw Paradise — or was shown Paradise — and reached for a cluster (of grapes or other fruit), and had I kept it, you would have eaten from it as long as this life remains." One cluster, feeding everyone until the end of the world: that is what "its provision is eternal" means in practice.
- Imam Muslim recorded that Jabir bin ʿAbdullah said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The people of Paradise eat and drink, and they do not need to blow their noses, or answer the call of nature, or urinate, for they pass the food excrements in belches, which smell like musk. They will be inspired to praise and glorify (Allah) as spontaneously as they breathe." Enjoyment there carries none of the indignity that trails enjoyment here — and remembrance of Allah becomes as effortless as breathing.
- Imams Ahmad and An-Nasaʼi recorded that Thumamah bin ʿUqbah said that he heard Zayd bin Arqam say: "A man from the People of the Scriptures came and said [to the Prophet ﷺ], 'O Abul-Qasim! You claim that the people of Paradise eat and drink?'" The Prophet ﷺ said: "Yes. By He in Whose Hand is Muhammad's life, a man among them will be given the strength of a hundred men in eating, drinking, sexual intercourse and appetite." The man then asked how one who eats and drinks could avoid needing to relieve the call of nature, when Paradise is pure. The Prophet ﷺ said: "One of them (residents of Paradise) relieves the call of nature through a sweat that emanates from the skin, with the scent of musk, and the stomach becomes empty again."

## ʿUqbā: the two ends

The passage closes: "this is the end (final destination) of those who have Taqwa, and the end (final destination) of the disbelievers is Fire." That is how Ibn Kathir's text renders *ʿuqbā* — what a road comes out at. The word is used twice in one breath, for both parties, with the same grammar. Everyone is travelling; everyone arrives somewhere.

Ibn Kathir observes that Allah often mentions the description of Paradise and the description of the Fire together, to make Paradise appealing and warn against the Fire. That is the architecture of this whole passage: the argument of ayah 33, the sentence of ayah 34, the Garden of ayah 35 — and the last line refusing to let you look at either destination on its own. He closes with "Not equal are the dwellers of the Fire and the dwellers of the Paradise. It is the dwellers of Paradise that will be successful" (59:20) — which quietly settles the question of what "success" is, after ayah 33 showed us people who were sure they had already found it.

## Living it

**Read ayah 33 about yourself.** The argument is aimed at idolaters, but its premise covers everybody: He takes charge of every person and knows all that he has earned. Ibn Kathir's supporting ayat — "He is with you wherever you may be," "He knows the secret and that which is yet more hidden" — leave no private corner. Nothing you do is unobserved, and nothing you do is unrecorded.

**Do not trust the feeling of being right.** The people in ayah 33 were not tormented by doubt; their plotting had been made fair-seeming to them, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says shaitan made their very ignorance look good in their sight, so that they took it for "achievement" and "success." Conviction is not evidence. Only what Allah has sent down as authority — as 53:23 puts it — settles anything.

**Aim at the end, not the stage.** The word *ʿuqbā* asks one question of every choice: where does this road come out? Those promised the Garden are named by a quality, not a lineage — "those who have Taqwa," whom Ibn Kathir's commentary also calls simply the righteous, pious believers. And the comfort in ayah 34 for anyone suffering now is real and hard-edged: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that the torment of this life is easier than the torment of the Hereafter, and Ibn Kathir adds the reason — the torment of this life ends. What the Garden gives — its provision and its shade — does not.

passages.title: Mixed reception, and the Arabic judgement
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat describe how the Qur'an was received by people who already had scripture in their hands — some rejoiced at it, while others rejected a part of it — and then tell the Prophet ﷺ what to say to them, and where he himself is headed. Ayah 37 then names what this Book is: a judgement of authority sent down in Arabic. And in the very next breath it warns against setting human opinion above the knowledge that has come from Allah.

## The setting

Just before this, in ayah 33, the Qur'an exposed the ignorance and irrationality of the disbelievers: they are, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, "short on sense" when they set inert idols alongside the pure Being of the One "who is watchful over everyone" and is the ultimate reckoner of everyone's deeds. And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes what lies behind that attitude: shaytan has made their very ignorance look good in their sight, so that they take it to be "achievement" and "success."

Ayah 36 now turns to those who were given the Book — and their reception splits in two.

## Ayah 36: the joy of those who recognised what they were hearing

**"Those to whom We have given the Book rejoice at what has been revealed to you."**

Ibn Kathir adds a short but decisive qualifier to the phrase *those to whom We have given the Book*: **and they adhere by it**. Merely inheriting a scripture is not what is being praised; these are the ones who actually held to what they were given. The heading over this section of the tafsir reads: "The Truthful Ones from among the People of the Scriptures rejoice at what Allah has revealed to Muhammad ﷺ."

And why the joy? Ibn Kathir gives the reason plainly: they rejoice at what was revealed to the Prophet ﷺ — that is, the Qur'an — **because they have evidence in their Books affirming the truth of the Qur'an and conveying the good news of its imminent revelation**. Their gladness was not a mood. It was recognition. They had been told in advance that this was coming, and then it came.

Ibn Kathir supports this with three passages from elsewhere in the Qur'an, and together they paint the character of these people:

- **"Those to whom We gave the Book recite it as it should be recited"** (2:121) — people who did not merely possess scripture but read it as it deserved to be read.
- **"And there are, certainly, among the People of the Scripture, those who believe in Allah"** (3:199) — the Qur'an refuses to flatten them into one hostile mass.
- And most vividly, 17:107–109: **"Say: Believe in it or do not believe"** … **"Truly, the promise of our Lord must be fulfilled"** … **"And they fall down on their faces weeping, and it increases their humility."** Ibn Kathir explains the middle line for us: their meaning is that *Allah's promise to us in our Books to send Muhammad ﷺ is true; it is certain and will surely come to pass and be fulfilled* — so all praise to our Lord, how truthful is His promise, all the thanks are due to Him.

Notice what their joy does to them in that last verse: it puts them on their faces, weeping, and *increases* their humility. Ibn Kathir brings this passage in support of the gladness ayah 36 is describing. Real gladness at revelation does not inflate a person; it bows him.

## The other reception: rejecting a part

**"But there are among the Aḥzāb those who reject a part of it."**

*Al-Aḥzāb* is rendered here as "the Confederates," and Ibn Kathir explains the phrase simply: **"There are those among the sects who disbelieve in some of what was revealed to you (O Muhammad)."**

Who are they? **Mujahid** said that *al-Aḥzāb* refers to the Jews and Christians, and that *those who reject a part thereof* means **"They reject a part of the truth that came down to you — O Muhammad."** Ibn Kathir notes that **similar was reported from Qatadah and from ʿAbd al-Rahman bin Zayd bin Aslam.**

Hold the two halves of ayah 36 side by side and you have the whole spectrum of response to revelation in a single line. Some rejoiced at what came down. Others took a portion and pushed the rest away. And the Qur'an does not describe that second response as a partial acceptance; its word for it is *reject*.

## What the Prophet ﷺ is told to say

**"Say: I am commanded only to worship Allah and not to join partners with Him. To Him I call, and to Him is my return."**

The answer to a mixed, sifting reception is not a compromise. It is a restatement of the one thing that cannot be adjusted. Ibn Kathir gives the sense in the Prophet's ﷺ own voice: *I was sent with the religion of worshipping Allah alone without partners, just as the Messengers before me.* The message is not a novelty; it stands in the same line as everything Allah sent before.

Then two short phrases close the verse, and Ibn Kathir glosses both:

- **إِلَيْهِ أَدْعُو** — *"To Him alone I call."* Ibn Kathir's gloss is one line: **"I call the people to His path."** The call is to Allah and to His path — not to the caller himself.
- **وَإِلَيْهِ مَآبِ** — *"and to Him is my return."* Ibn Kathir explains *maʾāb* as **final destination and destiny**. The one doing the calling is himself returning to the One he calls to.

## Ayah 37: "a judgement of authority in Arabic"

**"And thus have We sent it down as a judgement of authority in Arabic."** (Rendered elsewhere in this passage as: *"And so We have revealed it as an authority in Arabic."*)

The opening **"and thus"** ties this Book to every Book before it. Ibn Kathir unpacks it as Allah saying: *Just as We sent Messengers before you and revealed to them Divine Books from heaven, We sent down to you the Qur'an, a judgement of authority in Arabic.*

Two things are worth dwelling on here.

**What the Book is called.** The Qur'an describes itself with the language of judgement and authority. That is its own self-description, placed here directly after the ayah about people who received a part of it and rejected a part.

**That it came in Arabic.** Ibn Kathir reads this as a gift and a distinction: it was sent down in Arabic **"as an honour for you, and We preferred you among all people with this clear, plain and unequivocal Book."** Note the three words he uses for it — *clear, plain and unequivocal*. And he seals the point with another ayah about this Book: **"Falsehood cannot come to it from before it or behind it: it is sent down by the All-Wise, Worthy of all praise"** (41:42).

## The warning — and who it is really for

**"Were you to follow their desires after the knowledge which has come to you, then you will not have any walī (protector) or defender against Allah."**

Ibn Kathir's glosses here are brief and they sharpen the whole verse:

- **أَهْوَاءَهُم**, *their desires*, means **"their opinions."** That is worth pausing on. Set against a Book just described as a judgement of authority, the thing being followed in the alternative is not raw appetite but people's *views*.
- **بَعْدَمَا جَاءَكَ مِنَ الْعِلْمِ**, *after the knowledge which has come to you* — Ibn Kathir specifies its origin: **from Allah, all praise to Him.** The knowledge in question is not what someone worked out; it is what was given. And it is the having-received-it that raises the stakes.
- **مَا لَكَ مِنَ اللَّهِ مِن وَلِيٍّ وَلَا وَاقٍ** — **"then you will not have any walī (protector) or defender against Allah."** Two things denied at once, and denied absolutely: against Allah there is no protector and no defender.

The address is to the Prophet ﷺ, and it is put as a supposition — *were you to…* — which is part of what makes it so weighty.

And Ibn Kathir draws the lesson, aiming it very specifically. This part of the ayah, he writes, **"warns people of knowledge against following the paths of misguidance after they had gained knowledge in (and abided by) the Prophetic Sunnah and the path of Muhammad, may Allah's best peace and blessings be on him."** The warning lands hardest on the learned — on the one who has studied the Sunnah and then drifts after opinion.

## Living it

**Test your joy.** The heading over this passage in Ibn Kathir's tafsir calls those who rejoice "the truthful ones." When a verse or a ruling reaches you, what is the first movement in your chest — gladness that the matter has been settled by the One who knows, or a search for a way around it? The people praised here had evidence in their own Books, recognised the truth, and wept with it (17:109) — and it *increased* their humility.

**Watch the word "reject."** "They reject a part thereof" is not describing people with no scripture; Mujahid identifies them as scripture-people. Selective reading — keeping the parts that suit us and pushing away the rest — is what the ayah names, and it names it rejection.

**Know what you are calling people to.** When the reception is mixed, the instruction in ayah 36 is not to soften the core but to say it: *I am commanded only to worship Allah and not to join partners with Him. To Him I call, and to Him is my return.* Call to Allah's path, as Ibn Kathir glosses it — not to yourself — and remember where you are going.

**Guard knowledge with humility.** Ibn Kathir says plainly that this warning is for people of knowledge who have learned the Sunnah and the path of the Prophet ﷺ. If you have been given even a little sacred knowledge, this ayah is addressed to you before anyone else. And the only two rescues the verse mentions — a protector and a defender — are precisely the two it says will not be there.

passages.title: Messengers were men: signs by permission, conveyance only
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat answer an objection about what a messenger of Allah is supposed to be. The objectors wanted a messenger who was not an ordinary man, and who could produce verses and miracles whenever they asked. Ayah 38 replies by pointing to the messengers who came before — men with wives and children — and by stating that no messenger ever brought a sign except by Allah's leave, because everything has an appointed term already written. Ayah 39 widens that to the revealed Books and to the decree itself. Ayah 40 closes the circle: the Prophet's ﷺ assignment is delivery, not results; the reckoning belongs to Allah. The thread running through all three is a single line drawn between what belongs to Allah alone and what belongs to His Messenger.

## "A prophet should not be a man like us"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets out the mentality behind the objection. The disbelievers and polytheists assumed a prophet ought to be from some species other than human — an angel, say — so that his superiority over ordinary people would be obvious. The Qur'an refutes this in many places, because they had simply failed to grasp the wisdom behind sending messengers at all. A messenger is sent as a **model**, so that communities of human beings follow him and learn deeds and character like his. And a human being can only follow a fellow human. An angel feels no hunger or thirst, has no desires, does not sleep and does not tire; if people were commanded to take such a being as their pattern, they would have more on their hands than they could carry.

At the time of revelation the objection took its sharpest form around the Prophet's ﷺ marriages. Ayah 38 answers it head-on: how can you hold that a man who marries — once, or more than once — and has a household and children is thereby unfit for prophethood? What proof do you have for such a claim? It has always been Allah's practice that He makes His prophets masters of a household. The prophets who passed before — and you yourselves accept the prophethood of some of them — had wives and children. To imagine that this way of life is contrary to prophethood, or contrary to piety, is plain ignorance.

Ibn Kathir renders the sense as Allah addressing His Prophet ﷺ: *just as We have sent you, a prophet and a human, We sent the messengers before you from among mankind — men who ate food and walked in the markets — and We gave them wives and offspring.* And it is to the most honourable and final of the messengers that Allah said: **"Say: I am only a man like you. It has been revealed to me"** (18:110).

**From the Sunnah.** It is recorded in the Two Sahihs — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names them as the Sahih of al-Bukhari and Muslim — that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"As for me, I fast and break the fast, stand in prayer at night and sleep, eat meat and marry women; so whoever turns away from my Sunnah is not of mine."* Read it against the objection and it lands hard. The eating, the sleeping, the marrying are not concessions the Prophet ﷺ made to his humanity — they are his Sunnah. Whoever treats them as beneath religion has not risen above him; he has stepped outside his way.

## "It was not for a Messenger to bring a sign except by Allah's leave"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān identifies two hostile demands that opponents put to the prophets in every age, and put to the Prophet ﷺ in his:

**First**, that the rulings revealed in the Book should match their wishes. Their words are preserved in 10:15 — *"Bring a Qur'an other than this, or change it"* — meaning: one that does not forbid the worship of our idols; or else alter the rulings yourself, turning punishment into mercy and the unlawful into the lawful.

**Second**, that new miracles be produced on request. They had already seen open miracles, yet kept insisting: show us this or that particular sign, and then we may consider believing.

**The word āyah.** Lexically it means "sign". In Qur'anic usage it carries two established senses: a verse of the Qur'an, and a miracle. So some commentators read the phrase as: no prophet has the authority to introduce a verse into his Book on his own initiative. Others read it as: Allah has given no messenger the authority to produce a miracle when he chooses and as he chooses. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites Tafsir Ruh al-Maʿani that, on the basis of a rule of interpretation named there as *ʿumūm al-majāz*, both meanings could be taken and both explanations could be correct. The commentary names that rule without expounding it, but its verdict is plain enough: the two readings need not compete. Ibn Kathir's gloss brings out the second: no prophet could bring a miracle to his people except by Allah's permission and will, for this matter is decided by Allah alone, not by the prophets; He does what He wills and decides what He wills.

This is not a diminishing of the Messenger — it is a locating of authority. A prophet who could manufacture verses or conjure miracles at will would be a partner in the decision. He is not, and he never claimed to be.

## "For every term there is a decree" (end of ayah 38)

*Li-kulli ajalin kitāb.* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the two words. **Ajal** is the fixed time-frame allotted to a thing. **Kitāb** here functions as a verbal noun — "something written", prescribed. So: the time and the quantum of everything stand prescribed with Allah.
