He has prescribed in eternity that a particular person shall be born at a particular time, live so many days, travel to these places, do this as his life's work, and die then and there.

And in exactly the same way it is prescribed which revelations and rulings will be sent to which prophet at which time — for rulings suited to each era and each people is what reason and justice require — and prescribed too that a particular miracle will appear at the hands of a particular prophet at a particular hour.

Ibn Kathir says the same in his own words: for every appointed term there is a record that keeps it, and everything has a specific due measure with Allah — citing **"Know you not that Allah knows all that is in the heaven and on the earth? Verily, it is all in the Book. Verily, that is easy for Allah"** (22:70).

So the demand for a sign on request is not merely impertinent; it is confused. A miracle is not a trick the prophet carries in his sleeve. It is an event with an appointed hour, already written.

## Ayah 39 — "Allah blots out what He wills and confirms, and with Him is the Mother of the Book"

Two lines of interpretation run through the classical commentary, both traced to early authorities. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presents them side by side rather than choosing.

**1. Erasure and confirmation of revealed law (naskh).** Ibn Kathir opens with this: Allah blots out what He wills of the divinely revealed Books and confirms what He wills, until the Qur'an — revealed from Allah to His Messenger ﷺ — abrogated them all. Maʿārif attributes the reading to Saʿid ibn Jubayr, Qatadah and others: the codes and obligations sent to different peoples through different messengers were never all meant to last forever. As the conditions of peoples and the demands of the times change, Allah in His wisdom repeals whichever ruling He wills and retains whichever He wills — and the original Book with Him already records that this particular ruling was given for that particular period or those particular conditions, along with the ruling that would replace it.

That last point answers a doubt worth naming: does abrogating a law imply the Lawgiver had not correctly read the situation? No — because the abrogated ruling was known to Allah as temporary before ever He sent it down; its term was recorded from the start. Maʿārif offers a homely comparison: a physician examines a patient, sees his present symptoms and prescribes for them, already knowing what effect the medicine will have and that it will afterwards be replaced by a different prescription.

**2. Erasure and confirmation in the decree (qadar).** On the view of ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAbbas, reported by a group of leading commentators including Sufyan al-Thawri and Wakiʿ, the subject of the ayah is destiny. The provisions a person receives across his whole life, the comfort and distress that meet him, and their measures, are written before the creatures were created; then at a child's birth the angels are commanded to commit it to writing; and every Laylat al-Qadr a full roster of what is to happen in the coming year is handed to the angels. Mujahid says the same: during Laylat al-Qadr Allah decides what provisions and what disasters will occur in the coming year, and then brings forward, puts back, or blots out whatever He wills — while the Book containing the records of the happy and the wretched does not change. Mujahid's earlier comment on this ayah runs along the same line: the erasing and confirming applies to everything *"except life and death, misery and happiness"* — that is, faith and disbelief — *"for they do not change."*

**Conditional decree and final decree.** Maʿārif draws the two ends together. What is erased and confirmed is the register in the hands and the knowledge of the angels. Some of those decisions are contingent on a condition; when the condition does not occur, the decision does not take effect. Sometimes the condition is itself written and known to the angels — and sometimes it is not written at all, but exists in Allah's knowledge alone, which is why, when such a decision changes, everyone is left wondering. A destiny of this kind is called **taqdīr muʿallaq**, suspended or conditional destiny, and it is precisely there that the blotting out and the affirming keep operating. Above it stands **taqdīr mubram**, the final and definite decree, recorded in *umm al-kitāb*.

**Umm al-kitāb** translates word for word as "the Mother Book"; its literal sense, says Maʿārif, is **the Original Book** — a reference to the Preserved Tablet (*al-Lawh al-Mahfūz*), in which there can be no change or alteration. Written there are the decisions and commands that issue as the final outcome once the conditions have been met or the supplication answered. No one has access to it; nothing is deleted from it or added to it. After all the obliterating and affirming, what stands is what was with Allah all along.

**What this asks of you: pray anyway.** Ibn Kathir brings the hadith that supports the second reading: Imam Ahmad recorded that Thawban said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, *"A man might be deprived of a provision because of a sin that he commits; only supplication changes al-Qadar; and only birr — righteousness — can increase the life span."* An-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah also collected it. Ibn Kathir adds that there is a hadith recorded in the Sahih affirming that maintaining the ties of the womb increases the life span; Maʿārif names the Sahih of al-Bukhari for it, and cites a narration in the Musnad of Ahmad that obeying and serving one's parents increases one's years, and that nothing but duʿāʼ can avert what is destined.

The early Muslims turned this ayah into supplication. Mansur asked Mujahid about people who pray, *"O Allah, if my name is with the happy, affirm it among them; and if my name is among the wretched, remove it and place it among the happy"* — and Mujahid said: **"This supplication is good."** Al-Aʿmash narrated that Abu Waʼil, Shaqiq ibn Salamah, used to recite often: *"O Allah, if You wrote us among the wretched, remove that from us and write us among the blessed; and if You wrote us among the blessed, let us remain so — for surely You blot out and confirm what You will, and with You is the Mother of the Book."* Ibn Jarir at-Tabari collected this, and Ibn Kathir notes that similar statements were collected from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab and ʿAbdullah ibn Masʿud.

Hold the two halves together. Mujahid insists the register of the happy and the wretched does not change — and Mujahid calls that supplication good. There is no contradiction to untangle here so much as a posture to adopt: a believer is not asked to work out where his name stands. He is asked to ask. What the blotting out and the affirming reach is the Book of Destiny that is in the hands of the angels and in their knowledge; the Original Book with Allah, in which there can be no change or alteration, holds the decisions that issue as the final outcome once the conditions of deeds have been fulfilled or the duʿāʼ has been answered.

**A third angle, on how a life ends.** Al-ʿAwfi reported that Ibn ʿAbbas said of this ayah: a man may work in Allah's obedience for a time, then revert to disobedience and die misguided — *that* is what Allah blots out; and a man may work in disobedience, but goodness was destined for him, so he dies after returning to obedience — *that* is what Allah confirms. Saʿid ibn Jubayr said the ayah carries the meaning of another: **"Then He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills; and Allah is able to do all things"** (2:284).

## Ayah 40 — "Your duty is only to convey; on Us is the reckoning"

Ibn Kathir reads it as Allah speaking directly to His Messenger ﷺ: whether We show you part of the disgrace and humiliation We have promised your enemies in this life, or cause you to die before that — We sent you only to convey Allah's message to them, and in doing so you have fulfilled the mission laid upon you. Their reckoning and their recompense are Ours. He sets beside it the parallel in 88:21–26: **"So remind them — you are only one who reminds. You are not a dictator over them... Verily, to Us will be their return; then verily, for Us will be their reckoning."**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān hears in the ayah comfort and reassurance for the Prophet ﷺ. The promises Allah made him — that Islam will have the final victory and that disbelief and its people will be disgraced — will certainly come to pass. But he is told not to burden himself with *when*. It may happen within his lifetime; it may come after his departure from this world. Meanwhile there is already enough to steady the heart, in what the following ayah (41) points to: the lands of the disbelievers being cut back from their edges, passing under Muslim control. Ibn ʿAbbas glossed it as: do they not see that We are granting land after land to Muhammad ﷺ? Al-Hasan and Ad-Dahhak took it as the Muslims gaining the upper hand over the idolaters — as in **"And indeed We have destroyed towns round about you"** (46:27).

## Living it

**Do not be embarrassed by the humanity of the Prophet ﷺ.** He fasted and broke his fast, prayed at night and slept, ate meat and married. That is not a footnote to his prophethood; it is the pattern you were given to follow — and precisely because he was a man, following him is possible.

**Stop asking for terms.** The two ancient demands — that the religion be adjusted to suit us, and that a sign be produced on our schedule — still surface in modern dress. Ayah 38 answers both: the Messenger held no authority to edit revelation or to time a miracle, and every matter already has its appointed hour written.

**Make duʿāʼ, and make it seriously.** Provision, lifespan, ease and hardship are written; and the Prophet ﷺ taught that sin can withhold provision, that only supplication turns back the decree, and that only righteousness lengthens a life — with keeping the ties of kinship and honouring parents named among the deeds that do so. Ayah 39 is the ground under every prayer you have ever made for a decision you thought was already sealed.

**Convey, then let go of the outcome.** If the Messenger of Allah ﷺ himself was told that delivery is the whole of his assignment and the reckoning is Allah's, then no one after him carries the burden of producing results in another person's heart. That releases you from two weights at once: the anxiety of needing to succeed, and the bitterness of being refused.

# Sūrat al-Raʿd 41–43

These are the closing ayat of Sūrat al-Raʿd, and the objection they answer is stated in the passage itself: *"You are not a Messenger."* Ibn Kathir notes that ayah 43 was revealed in Makkah, so this denial was being said to the Prophet ﷺ's face. The passage answers in three moves — look at the land (ayah 41), look at those who came before (ayah 42), look at who is qualified to testify (ayah 43) — and what holds them together is a single reassurance to the Prophet ﷺ: the outcome is not your burden, it is already visibly in motion, and Allah Himself stands as witness.

## The frame: your job is to deliver, Ours is the reckoning

The immediately preceding ayah sets the tone the whole passage inherits. Ibn Kathir paraphrases Allah's address to His Messenger ﷺ: *"Whether We show you"* — O Muhammad — *"part of the disgrace and humiliation We have promised your enemies in this life, or cause you to die"* before that, *"your duty is only to convey"*; you have been sent to convey Allah's message to them, and by doing so you will have fulfilled the mission ordained on you. *"And on Us is the reckoning"* — their reckoning and recompense are Ours. He cites the same division of labour from Sūrat al-Ghāshiya:

> *"So remind them — you are only one who reminds. You are not a dictator over them — save the one who turns away and disbelieves. Then Allah will punish him with the greatest punishment. Verily, to Us will be their return, then verily, for Us will be their reckoning."* (88:21–26)

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads ayah 40 as comfort and assurance. The Prophet ﷺ has been given the good news that Islam will have the final victory and that disbelief and the disbelievers will be disgraced — that promise "shall come to pass definitely." But, it adds, "you should not concern yourself as to when this victory will finally come." It may happen within his lifetime; it may come after his departure from this world. The obligation is attached to the conveying, not to the timetable.

That is the doorway into ayah 41. Having set aside the question of *when*, the passage immediately hands him something he can already see.

## Ayah 41 — the land that keeps getting smaller

**"See they not…"** The ayah opens as a question, and it is a question about what is in front of their eyes. It does not ask them to accept a claim; it points to something already happening. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws exactly this out: "For your peace of heart, even this much is enough that you are continuously witnessing that We are causing the lands of the disbelievers to keep being sliced off their sides."

**"That We gradually reduce the land from its outlying borders."** Note the word *gradually*, and note that it is the *borders* that go. This is not described as one dramatic event but as a steady reduction from the sides inward. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it plainly — "these sides pass on under Muslim control whereby the land occupied by them keeps reducing in area… a day will come when the final phase of their victory shall stand completed."

The early authorities read the ayah along the same line:

- **Ibn ʿAbbās** glossed it as a question put to the deniers themselves: "See they not that We are granting land after land to Muhammad ﷺ?"
- **Al-Ḥasan and al-Ḍaḥḥāk** commented that this ayah refers to Muslims gaining the upper hand over the idolaters.

Ibn Kathir places alongside it another ayah with the same geography: *"And indeed We have destroyed towns round about you"* (46:27) — again, what lies *round about*, at the edges, rather than at the centre.

**"And Allah judges, there is none to put back His judgement, and He is swift at reckoning."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān summarises this closing clause: "The command is in the very hands of Allah Taʿālā. There is no one who can avert this command. And He is the One swift at reckoning."

Notice how the word *reckoning* has now landed twice in two ayat — first in ayah 40, where it lifts the weight off the Prophet ﷺ ("and on Us is the reckoning"), and now at the end of ayah 41, where it stands over those who reject him. The same divine prerogative that relieves the one who conveys is the one closing in on those who refuse.

And notice what the passage does and does not promise. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān has already closed the question of the date — it may be in his lifetime, it may be after. What is guaranteed instead is ownership: the command is in Allah's hands, and no one can avert it.

## Ayah 42 — every plot ever laid, and who actually owns planning

**"And verily, those before them did devise plots."** Ibn Kathir supplies both the target and the aim: those plots were laid against their Messengers, and what the plotters wanted was to expel them from their land. The ayah sets the present rejecters against a precedent — *those before them* — and Ibn Kathir tells us how the precedent ended: "but Allah devised plots against the disbelievers and gave the good end to those who fear Him."

**"But all planning is Allah's."** The word used of their plotting is used again, immediately, of Allah — and the two passages Ibn Kathir cites do the same thing, deliberately holding the same word on both sides of the sentence:

> *"And (remember) when the disbelievers plotted against you to imprison you, or to kill you, or to get you out; they were plotting and Allah too was plotting; and Allah is the Best of those who plot."* (8:30)

> *"So they plotted a plot, and We planned a plan, while they perceived not. Then see how was the end of their plot! Verily, We destroyed them and their nation, all together."* (27:50–51)

Then comes the clause that dismantles the whole enterprise: **"He knows what every person earns."** Ibn Kathir's comment is that He alone knows all secrets and concealed thoughts, and He will reckon each person according to his work. The translation of this ayah renders the earlier plotting as *secretly* planned — and secrecy is the one asset a plotter cannot do without. Ibn Kathir's gloss removes it: there are no secrets and no concealed thoughts before Allah. Whatever is being arranged in rooms you will never enter is already fully known.

**"And the disbelievers will know who gets the good end."** Ibn Kathir notes that this word is recited in two ways: *al-Kāfir*, "the disbeliever," and *al-Kuffār*, "the disbelievers," according to another way of reciting.

He then spells out the question the phrase leaves hanging — who will earn the ultimate and final victory, they or the followers of the Messengers? — and answers it: the followers of the Messengers will earn the good end in this life and the Hereafter, "all thanks and praise is due to Allah."

Note the verb: they *will know*. It is not offered as a proposition for debate. It is a result they will one day be brought to see.

## Ayah 43 — "You are not a Messenger"

The sūrah ends by quoting the rejecters' bluntest line. Ibn Kathir renders it: the disbelievers reject you and say, *"You are not a Messenger"* — from Allah. And the reply the Prophet ﷺ is instructed to give is not a counter-argument but a summoning of witnesses.

**Witness one: Allah.** *"Say: Sufficient as a witness between me and you is Allah."* Ibn Kathir unfolds it: say, 'Allah is sufficient for me and He is the witness over me and over you. He is witness that I have conveyed the Message from Him, and over you, O rejecters, to the falsehood that you invent.' It is a testimony that cuts in two directions at once — the same divine gaze that certifies the conveying is registering the invention.

**Witness two: "and those too who have knowledge of the Scripture."** Here the commentators differ, and Ibn Kathir walks through the views rather than flattening them:

- **Mujāhid** said this refers to ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām. Ibn Kathir holds this opinion "not plausible," and gives a chronological reason: this ayah was revealed in Makkah, whereas ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām embraced Islam soon after the Prophet ﷺ emigrated to Madīnah.
- **Ibn ʿAbbās**, in the narration of al-ʿAwfī, said it refers to the Jews and Christians — and Ibn Kathir calls this "a more suitable explanation."
- **Qatādah** said that among them are ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām, Salmān (al-Fārisī) and Tamīm al-Dārī.

Ibn Kathir then states what he holds to be **the correct view**: the phrase refers to the scholars of the People of the Scriptures who find the description of Muhammad ﷺ in their own Books, and the good news of his advent that was conveyed to them by their own Prophets. He supports this with two further passages — the description of *"the Prophet who can neither read nor write, whom they find written with them in the Tawrāh and the Injīl"* (7:156–157), and the challenge, *"It is not a sign to them that the learned scholars of the Children of Israel knew it (as true)?"* (26:197). "There are similar Ayat," he adds, "that affirm that the scholars of the Children of Israel know this fact from their divinely revealed Books."

So the reply to "you are not a Messenger" is not a defence of self. It is a pointing outward: Allah is witness — and there are men of knowledge who already hold the description and the announcement in the Books they received before this one.

## Living it

**Deliver, don't dictate.** Ayah 40 draws the line and ayat 41–43 keep it: conveying is yours, the reckoning is Allah's. Ibn Kathir's citation is the standard — from the passage he quotes, "you are only one who reminds. You are not a dictator over them" (88:21–26).

**Do not tie your peace of heart to the date.** The sign offered in ayah 41 is a gradual one — borders, not a single stroke. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's counsel to the Prophet ﷺ is the counsel to us: the promise is definite, but "you should not concern yourself as to when this victory will finally come." The command is in Allah's hands, and no one can avert it.

**Stop fearing the schemers.** People plotted against the Messengers before, and wanted them expelled from their land. Ayah 42 tells you the ceiling on all of it: a plot needs concealment, and Allah "alone knows all secrets and concealed thoughts."

**Let Allah be your witness when your integrity is denied.** The Prophet ﷺ was told to his face that he was no Messenger. He was not instructed to argue; he was instructed to say *"Sufficient as a witness between me and you is Allah."* When people have decided in advance, that sentence is both a defence and a release.

*Ibn Kathir closes his commentary on the sūrah here: "This is the end of Sūrat al-Raʿd, and all praise is due to Allah and all favors are from Him."*
